From the owner
Drafty doors and windows in Michigan homes, and why they show up every fall - The first cold morning of October tells you a lot about your house. You notice the chill by the front door, the curtain that moves on its own and the bedroom that never quite warms up. Drafty doors and windows are the most common comfort complaint we hear from Southeast Michigan homeowners, and most of them can be fixed with carpentry rather than a replacement quote. Our draft sealing service exists because the fix is usually smaller than people fear. This guide walks through every place cold air gets past a door or a window, what you can check yourself on a Saturday and what calls for a trained set of hands. It covers entry doors, storm doors, patio doors, double-hung sashes, sills, trim and the caulk lines that hold it all together. When a section points to a job our Wright’s Repairs division handles, we link to it so you can see exactly what the visit includes. We are a design-build firm based in Ypsilanti, and over the years our crews have worked in older plaster-wall homes in Ann Arbor, postwar ranches in Westland and newer colonials in Canton. The draft problems look different in each, but the causes repeat. Worn seals, doors that moved out of square, sills that rotted from the bottom and caulk that gave up years ago account for nearly everything we find on a winterizing visit for Michigan homes. How Michigan housing stock shapes the problem...

What we build

Renovation, done end to end

Design, permitting, construction, and finish work under one roof. Six specialized crews. One project manager per home, start to walkthrough.

From $75K
Kitchen remodeling
Full gut renos, layout reworks, and additions. Custom cabinetry, stone counters, integrated appliance plans. Cabinet orders go in the week your selections are signed, so the long-lead item is never the thing holding up your build.
Explore kitchens
From $40K
Bathroom renovation
Primary suites, wet rooms, half baths. Heated floors are not a luxury in a Michigan February, they are the reason you stop dreading the tile. Every shower pan gets a flood test before anything goes on the wall.
Explore bathrooms
From $70K
Basement finishing
Family rooms, home theaters, in-law suites, wet bars. We check the perimeter drain, the sump, and the grade outside before we frame a single wall down there. A bedroom needs a code-compliant egress window, and we cut it.
Explore basements
From $185K
Home additions
Second-story builds, primary suite additions, ADUs, in-law suites. Engineered drawings and full permitting handled. In-law suites with a first-floor bath are the fastest-growing request we get across all six counties.
Explore additions
From $45K
Decks and outdoor
Composite and hardwood decks, three-season rooms, covered patios. Footings go below the frost line and framing gets sized for snow load, not just for the seventy-degree day it was built on.
Explore outdoor living
From $350K
Whole-home renovation
Down-to-studs rebuilds, historic restoration, full-floor reworks. Phased construction so your family stays in-home when possible, with one schedule covering every trade. On the Craftsman and Victorian stock around Ann Arbor we mill trim profiles to match what is already in the house, not the closest thing on a shelf.
Explore whole home

Service area

Everything inside an hour of the shop

Six counties, all dispatched from one building on Platt Road in Ypsilanti. We drew the line at about an hour because a crew that leaves at 6:45 should be working by 8:00, not sitting on I-696. Each county runs its own permit timelines and its own inspectors, and we hold the license in all six. See every project we have finished.

Headquarters

Southeast Michigan housing stock

What we find behind the walls

The year your house was built predicts most of your budget. We have opened walls in every one of these eras, in every one of these neighborhoods, and the surprises stopped being surprises a long time ago. Find your house below and you will know what we are looking for before we get there.

Before 1920
Balloon frame and plaster

Ann Arbor's Old West Side and Water Hill. Ypsilanti's Normal Park and Depot Town. Downtown Plymouth and Northville. Grosse Pointe's older blocks.

Knob-and-tube wiring still live in a ceiling box
Plaster and lath over rough-sawn studs on irregular centers
No subfloor insulation, and often no subfloor
Galvanized supply lines choked down to a pencil
A coal chute bricked into the basement wall

Exterior changes inside Ann Arbor's historic districts go to the Historic District Commission before they reach the building department. Budget four to eight weeks for that review, and design to it from the start rather than appealing later.

1920s to 1940s
Brick bungalows and colonials

Royal Oak, Berkley and Ferndale's brick bungalow grid. Birmingham's older colonials. Dearborn and the Wayne County streetcar blocks.

Cast-iron waste stacks, sometimes scaled half shut
Sixty-amp service in a fuse box behind a door
Arched plaster openings worth every hour it takes to save
One original bathroom, five feet by seven
Solid oak floors under three layers of vinyl

These are the best bones in the region. The kitchens are small because 1928 wanted them small, and opening one to the dining room is almost always a load-bearing conversation. A flush beam and two point loads to the basement is the usual answer in the Royal Oak bungalow blocks.

1950s to 1970s
Ranches and split-levels

Livonia, Westland, Canton and Belleville. Warren and Sterling Heights out through Macomb. Southfield and the older Farmington streets.

Copper supply, which is the good news
Aluminum branch wiring in houses built about 1965 to 1973
Original single-pane aluminum sliders
Undersized returns, so the back bedroom never warms up
A load-bearing center wall a beam can usually replace

Eight-foot ceilings make these feel smaller than they are. Pulling the center wall and running the ceiling flat changes the whole floor for less than most people expect. If we find aluminum branch circuits, they get pigtailed with approved connectors and that line item goes in the proposal, not a change order.

1980s to 2000s
Big footprints, tired finishes

Novi, Northville Township, South Lyon and Brighton. Rochester Hills, Troy and West Bloomfield. Saline and Pittsfield's newer subdivisions.

Builder-grade oak everywhere, in good structural shape
Two-story foyers that owners now want closed in
Original decks at the end of their service life
Polybutylene or early CPVC in a narrow band of builds
Whirlpool tubs nobody has filled since 2009

Structurally these are the easiest houses we work on, which means the money goes where you can see it. The common project in the Novi subdivisions and the Rochester Hills builds is a kitchen and primary bath together, because the layouts are already right and the finishes are twenty-five years old.

How it works

Four phases. No surprises.

From the first call to final walkthrough, every project runs on the same documented process. You always know what comes next, and you always know who to call.

01
 / 04

One project manager owns your house from contract to warranty visit. Not a rotating cast, not a dispatcher. The same person who walked your basement in February is the one handing you the care guide in May.

Week 1
Discovery call

A working conversation about scope, budget, and what you actually want the space to do. We will tell you on that call if your number and your wish list do not meet. No sales pressure, and no reason to be polite about it.

Weeks 2–3
Design and proposal

In-home measure, 3D renderings, materials selection, and a fixed-scope proposal with real numbers. You see the room before you commit to it, and you see every line item that adds up to the total.

Build phase
Construction

Zip-wall barriers up, ram board down, photos in JobTread every day so you can check the site from a meeting. Your home stays livable wherever we can manage it, and we tell you straight when we cannot.

Final week
Walkthrough and warranty

Punch list, final inspection, care guide, warranty packet. The one-year visit goes on the calendar before we pull the last truck off your driveway, so nobody has to remember to schedule it.

See the full process

Wright's Repairs

Have a smaller project in mind? Let's chat!

Most people assume a company that frames additions will not come out to rehang a door. For three years they were right. We turned down hundreds of homeowners who had already hired us for something bigger, because a two-hour job does not fit inside a twelve-week build.

Wright's Repairs is what we did about it. Its own technicians, its own van, its own schedule, and the same builder's license and finish standard that stands behind a six-figure kitchen. More than sixty jobs, each written out on a page of its own with the scope, the limits and what moves the price.

See the full repair catalog
Call (734) 251-4187

After

One
One thing broke

A toilet running all night, a cracked ceiling, a deck board gone soft underfoot, a deadbolt that stopped turning. Send photos and a few seconds of video, get a written range and a ceiling, then get a date. No morning lost to an estimate visit.

Two
A list you have been saving up

Most people call with five or six things at once, and that is the shape that works best for both sides. Twenty packages bundle the ones that tend to arrive together: a move, a new baby, an inspection report with fourteen items, the first hard freeze.

Three
The job that turns out to be bigger

Sometimes a patch visit finds a remodel. Three failing fixtures in one bathroom is a renovation argument, not a repair one. The crew that would quote it works in the same building, so nothing gets diagnosed twice and the handoff costs you nothing.

bathroom fixtures and tile
doors, locks and hardware
drywall, plaster and texture
baseboard, shelving and railings
deck boards and railings
squeaks, gaps and floor patches
sashes, balances and glazing
one room, one ceiling, one stairwell
cabinet doors and drawer slides
fixtures, fans and lanterns
valves, traps and supply lines
downspouts and storm damage
the twenty repair packages

Repairs runs a tighter radius than our renovation crews, about thirty minutes by road from the shop at 7101 Platt Road in Ypsilanti. Outside that ring, ask anyway and you will get a straight answer.

Who you actually work with

A company small enough that the founder still answers the phone
Design before demolition

Most contractors treat design as a step they have to get through. We treat it as the work. Before a single wall comes down you will see 3D renderings, signed-off material specs, and a fixed-scope build calendar. It is the heart of our design-build method.

It costs more time upfront. It costs less in change orders, surprise budgets, and the regret of finishing a project and realizing the layout still does not quite work.

Built for the long version of the story

Trends are easy. A space that still feels right in twelve years is harder. We pull from the era of the house, the bones of the neighborhood, and the way you actually live now to find the version that ages well.

That is why we say no to certain finishes, even when clients ask for them. If a choice is going to look dated before the warranty runs out, you will hear it from us first. Honesty is part of the work.

The kitchen that gets remodeled twice in twenty years is more expensive than the one designed correctly the first time. Our entire job is making sure you only do this once.

The difference

Why six-figure clients choose us

Same scope, same Michigan market. Here is what changes when you hire a design-build firm instead of a general contractor. See how our process works.

Category	Typical contractor	Wright's Renovations
Estimate process	Verbal range over the phone. Real number comes after demo.	Fixed-scope proposal with line-item materials and labor before contract.
Communication	Text the foreman. Sometimes a reply. Often not.	JobTread platform: daily photos, real-time schedule, every doc and invoice in one place.
Change orders	15–20% of contract value, industry average.	Under 5%. Most projects close at the original signed number.
Design support	Bring your own designer, or pick from this catalog.	In-house designer, 3D renderings, materials sourcing. Included in scope, not extra.
Site condition	Dust everywhere. Floor protection optional.	Zip-wall dust barriers, ram board floor protection, daily clean-up. Non-negotiable.
After punch list	Call if anything comes up. Phone goes to voicemail.	One-year warranty walkthrough scheduled at handoff. We come back.

About

Design-build in Southeast Michigan
One team plans it. The same team builds it.

Most renovations split design and construction between two companies that have never met. Wright’s Renovations does both under one roof, one contract, and one phone number you call when you have a question.

Start your project
See our work
one
team

Designer, project manager, and crew sit on the same side of the table.

one
contract

A single agreement covers drawings and the build. No handoff.

one
number to call

When something comes up, you already know who answers.

What design-build means
The plans and the build answer to the same people.

In the older way of working, you hire a designer to draw your kitchen remodel, then take those drawings out to contractors for bids. The designer never sees a job site. The builder never sat in your first meeting. When the framing meets the drawing and they disagree, you are the one stuck between them.

Design-build closes that gap. The people who price the work helped draw it, so the budget you approve is the budget that gets built.

That single line of accountability is the whole point. A wall that costs more to move than expected gets flagged during design, on paper, before anyone swings a hammer. The same logic carries through every service, from a bathroom renovation to a full home addition.

How a project moves
a
We sit down together

Goals, budget, and the parts of your house that drive you up the wall.

b
We design and price as one step

Every drawing carries a real number, not a placeholder.

c
We build what you approved

Same team, daily photos, the schedule you signed off on.

d
We walk it with you

You sign off on the finished room, not a punch list of excuses.

One team. One contract. One number to call.
The honest comparison
The split approach versus design-build

Both can produce a good room. The difference is who carries the risk when the drawing and the job site disagree.

 
Design, then bid, then build
Design-build with Wright’s
Who is accountable
Designer and builder point at each other
One team owns the whole outcome
When you learn the real cost
After drawings are done and bids come back
During design, on every decision
How phases run
Each one waits for the last to finish
Design and prep overlap, so you start sooner
Your paperwork
Separate contracts with each company
A single contract with clear terms
When problems surface
On site, as expensive change orders
On paper, before the build begins
Why it works for you
What the single line of accountability actually buys

The structure is plumbing. These are the things you notice while living through a renovation.

You start sooner

Because design and pre-construction overlap, prep begins before the last drawing is signed.

The budget holds

Costs are attached to choices while you are still choosing, so the final number rarely surprises you.

One person knows everything

Your project manager has the same dashboard you do. No re-explaining your house to a stranger.

The ideas are buildable

Designs are checked against framing, plumbing, and code as they are drawn, not after they are approved.

Fewer surprises mid-build

The hard questions get answered during design, where changing your mind costs an eraser, not a demo crew.

One schedule, kept honest

The same team that drew the timeline is the team building to it, so a slip in one phase is caught in the next.

The
process
Four phases, one team

You always know which phase you are in and who to ask about it.

phase one
Discovery

We learn the budget, the timeline, and what the space needs to do that it does not do now.

phase two
Design and price

Drawings and dollar figures grow together, so you approve a plan you can actually afford.

phase three
Build

Daily photos, a live schedule, and one project manager from demo to the last coat of paint.

phase four
Walkthrough

We go room by room together, fix anything you flag, and hand over a space that matches the plan.

Built for Michigan houses
We only build here.

Working one region deep means we already know the soil, the permit desks, and the way a 1920s Ann Arbor foundation behaves in February. A firm flown in from out of state finds that out on your dime. Explore our full range of remodeling services or see what we do in Macomb County and beyond.

Climate-aware design

Plans that account for Michigan’s freeze-thaw swings and humidity, not a generic spec sheet.

Older-home know-how

Updates that respect a house’s original character while bringing it up to how people live now.

Permit relationships

Standing familiarity with building departments across all six counties we serve.

Local ground truth

What the soil and water table mean for foundations, drainage, and basement finishing.

Six counties, one crew

Home remodeling, planned as one house.

Most remodels start with one room and spill into the next. Wright’s Renovations draws the whole house first, then builds it in one order with one crew. The kitchen, the baths and the basement finish like they belong to the same home. It’s home remodeling for Ann Arbor, Ypsilanti and the towns around them, run out of one building on Platt Road.

Contact us now for a free quote

Why a whole home remodel runs better on one plan

Four rooms remodeled one after another rarely add up to one house. Kitchens, bathrooms and basements share wiring, plumbing stacks and framing, so the order they’re built in decides how many times a wall gets opened. Wright’s maps the entire house first, then sets that order. Phasing a whole-home renovation follows the same rule: the plan comes first, and the phase lines get drawn on top of it.

All at once

One drawing set and one permit package cover the whole house. Systems go in before finishes, so the panel, the main plumbing lines and the ductwork get done once and serve every room that follows. Trades move through the house in a single pass, inspections get grouped by trade, and one punch list closes the job. Doing it all at once is often a little more efficient per dollar, as long as the family can live with the disruption.

Either way, the people who draw the plan are the people who build it. One project manager owns the house from contract to warranty visit. If you’re weighing design-build against a general contractor, that single line of accountability is the difference that shows up most on a whole house.

Rooms a home remodeling plan can include

A whole-house plan can pull in any of the rooms below, and on a wide screen the small house beside the list lights up where each one sits. The prices are the published starting points for a typical scope, and the real number comes from your own drawings. The remodeling cost calculator gets you closer before anyone visits. The house at the top of this page is built from real versions of most of these rooms.

Stairs, trim and the rooms between
Priced by scope
Kitchen remodeling
From $75,000

The kitchen usually sets the schedule for everything around it, because it’s the room a family can least live without. Kitchen remodeling covers layout, cabinets, lighting and plumbing, and an island or a countertop and backsplash change can be priced on its own.

Bathroom remodeling
From $40,000

Primary baths, hall baths and powder rooms get sequenced around the kitchen so the family isn’t left without both at once. Bathroom remodeling covers tile, vanities, ventilation and layout. A tub can give way to a walk-in shower, the way it did in the Plymouth Township primary bath.

Basement finishing
From $70,000

A finished lower level adds living space without adding a roof. Basement finishing handles framing, insulation, lighting and baths below grade, and an egress window is what turns a spare room down there into a legal bedroom.

Home additions
From $185,000

When the house has run out of room, an addition grows the footprint. It ties into the original roofline, so it reads as part of the house rather than a box bolted onto the back. Home additions range from second-story additions to bump-outs that borrow a few feet for a kitchen or a bath.

Exterior remodeling
Priced by scope

Siding, windows and doors are the parts of a remodel the neighbors see and the parts Michigan weather tests hardest. Exterior remodeling runs in the warm months, often pairing window replacement with siding repair and replacement on the same walls.

Decks and outdoor living
From $45,000

A deck, a screened porch or a sunroom usually lands on the back of the house, where the kitchen meets the yard. Deck building and the rest of outdoor living get scheduled for the building season, and they can share a phase with an addition.

Mudrooms and laundry
Priced by scope

The back entry takes a beating in a Michigan winter, between boots, salt and the dog. A mudroom with real storage and a laundry room that isn’t in the basement are small scopes that change how the house runs every day.

Home offices
Priced by scope

A spare bedroom, a corner of the basement or a new room can become a home office with its own lighting, its own wiring and a door that closes. The green office at the top of this page sits in a 19-by-23-foot second story built over an Ann Arbor garage.

In-law and guest suites
Priced by scope

A suite for a parent, a grown kid or long visits can sit on the main floor, in the basement or in an addition. An in-law suite needs its own bath and an easy way in, so it gets planned with the rest of the house instead of squeezed in later.

Stairs, trim and the rooms between
Priced by scope

Hallways, staircases and trim tie the remodeled rooms together, and they’re the first thing that looks dated once everything around them is new. Custom carpentry covers railings, built-ins and millwork, like the Ypsilanti staircase at the top of this page.

Whole house renovation for the house you already have

Southeast Michigan’s houses span well over a century, and each era hides different problems behind the walls. The plan starts with the house as it stands, which is why Wright’s sorts its work by Michigan home type before it sorts by room.

Before 1940
1945 to 1979
1980 to today
Before 1940
Historic homes

Victorian houses, Craftsman bungalows, foursquares, Tudors and farmhouses carry original detail worth keeping. A historic home renovation usually means plaster and lath, knob-and-tube wiring and cast-iron drains, so the systems work gets scoped before anyone picks tile.

1945 to 1979
Mid-century homes

Ranches, split-levels and Cape Cods were framed for a different way of living, with closed kitchens and small baths. Mid-century homes get remodeled around how families live now. A ranch home addition or a Cape Cod addition can give a tight floor plan the room it never had.

1980 to today
Modern homes

Newer subdivision houses have good bones and builder-grade finishes that often wear out together. Modern home renovation tends to be a finishes and layout job: soffits out, kitchens opened, carpet swapped for hardwood. The Plymouth Township house further down this page got all three.

In any era, demolition tends to reveal that plumbing and wiring rarely sit where the original drawings expected. That’s why it pays to read up on what older houses hide, and why the next section covers how surprises get priced.

What a whole house remodel costs in Southeast Michigan

Whole-home renovations start from $350,000. That covers down-to-studs rebuilds, historic restorations and full-floor reworks, built in phases when the family needs to stay home. A smaller multi-room job costs less. The Ann Arbor kitchen that grew into most of a floor came to about $165,000 for 12 line items, inside and out, under one contract.

Pricing works the same way on every home remodeling job, whatever its size. The proposal is a fixed price, and nothing changes without your approval. Change orders run under 5 percent, and most projects close at the original signed number. When a wall hides something, you get photos, three priced fixes and a recommendation within 24 hours.

Each cost calculator builds a range for one part of the house. The renovation budget planning guide shows how to stack them into one number, and return by project type shows which rooms tend to pay back at resale.

Paying for a whole-house remodel

Wright’s works with two lenders so the financing fits the size of the job. Acorn Finance arranges unsecured loans from $1,000 to $100,000 with a soft credit pull and no lien on the home. Mortgage Center handles the larger scopes: renovation mortgages, one-time close construction loans and cash-out refinances, which take four to eight weeks to close. The remodel financing page compares both, and no dealer fees get built into a Wright’s quote.

Living at home while the work moves through the house

Staying in the house through a whole home remodel is possible, and the plan gets built around it. Phases get ordered to avoid tearing out the kitchen and the only full bath at the same time. The loudest, dustiest work gets scheduled with some thought for who’s home. The guide to living through a renovation covers the practical side in more detail.

What protects the house

Zip-wall dust barriers go up and ram board goes down before demolition starts, and the site gets cleaned at the end of every day. A single project manager stays with the house from contract to warranty visit, so there’s one person to call when the plan changes or the dog needs to stay in.

How you’ll know what happened today

Every evening, the foreman posts a daily log in JobTread with photos of the day’s work, what got done and what happens tomorrow. Every Friday, the project manager sends a weekly update with the schedule chart, the budget position, any decisions needed from you and the plan for the coming week. Every document and invoice sits in the same place, and the Wright’s project process page walks through each step.

How a Wright’s remodel runs from first call to final walkthrough

Every Wright’s remodel moves through the same six stages, and the first two take very little of your time. A whole house follows the same path as a single bath; the build stage just runs longer. Wright’s pulls every permit under its own Michigan builder license and schedules each inspection around the build calendar.

15 minutes
Discovery

A phone call about the house, the rooms and the budget you have in mind.

02
60 to 90 minutes
Consultation

An in-home consultation with measurements and honest pricing.

03
Two to four weeks
Proposal

Drawings and a fixed price, itemized line by line.

04
Three to six weeks
Pre-construction

Permits, selections and ordering, so crews aren’t waiting on parts.

05
Four to 16 weeks
Build

Daily logs, Friday updates and one project manager on the house.

06
One day on site
Reveal

A room-by-room punch list, closed before the crew leaves, with a one-year walkthrough on the calendar.

On a whole house, expect the proposal and pre-construction stages to sit toward the long end of their ranges, since there’s more to draw and more to select. Connor Wright’s letter before the first meeting explains what to expect from that first visit.

A whole home remodel in Plymouth Township, before and after

This Plymouth Township house still wore its original wallpaper, brass and carpet in every room. Crews pulled the kitchen soffits for full-height cabinets and reframed the wall between the kitchen and the dining room. In the primary bath, the tub gave way to a walk-in shower behind frameless glass, and every stair railing came back in oak over black metal balusters.

Why kitchen remodeling
Transform the heart of your home

Your kitchen should inspire you to cook, gather, and create. An outdated layout, worn countertops, or cramped workspace can make even simple meals feel like a chore. A thoughtfully redesigned kitchen changes how you experience your entire home.

Whether you’re dreaming of custom cabinetry with soft-close drawers, a stunning kitchen island for entertaining, or professional-grade appliance installation, Wright’s Renovations brings the expertise to make your culinary vision reality. Our design-build approach means one team handles everything from initial design through final installation, eliminating the coordination headaches that plague traditional renovation projects. Two built examples: an Ann Arbor kitchen opened up alongside a rebuilt stair, and a Belleville kitchen taken back to the studs.

Design-build simplicity

One contract, one team, one point of accountability from concept to completion

6-10 week timeline

Detailed planning and specialized crews mean faster, more predictable builds

Real-time project portal

Daily photos, budget tracking, and schedule updates at your fingertips

Price-match guarantee

The quote you approve is the price you pay, with no surprise change orders

Kitchen remodeling services
Complete kitchen transformation services

From minor updates that refresh your space to complete gut renovations that reimagine your kitchen’s entire layout, we offer comprehensive services tailored to your vision, timeline, and budget.

Most Popular
Custom cabinetry

Cabinets define your kitchen’s style and functionality. Our custom cabinet solutions include soft-close hinges and drawers, pull-out organizers, and premium finishes from painted shaker to natural wood grain. We work with top manufacturers and local craftsmen to deliver the exact look you envision, whether that’s sleek modern flat-panel or timeless raised-panel traditional.

Starting from $15,000
Learn more
Countertops & backsplashes

Transform your workspace with premium countertops in quartz, granite, marble, or butcher block. We precision-cut and install with invisible seams, then complement with stunning backsplash tile, from classic subway to bold geometric patterns.

From $5,000
Learn more
Kitchen islands

The modern kitchen’s social hub. Our custom kitchen islands add prep space, storage, and seating while potentially housing sinks, cooktops, or built-in appliances. We design islands that work with your kitchen’s traffic flow.

From $8,000
Learn more
Kitchen flooring

Durable, beautiful, and easy to clean. We install kitchen flooring in hardwood, luxury vinyl plank, tile, and engineered options designed to withstand heavy foot traffic, spills, and Michigan’s tracked-in seasons while complementing your design vision.

From $4,000
Learn more
Kitchen lighting

Layer your light for function and ambiance. Our kitchen lighting designs combine recessed task lighting, statement pendants over islands, and under-cabinet LED strips that illuminate workspaces without shadows. Dimmable controls let you set the mood.

From $2,500
Learn more
Appliance installation

Professional-grade or family-friendly, we help you select and install kitchen appliances that match your cooking style. From built-in refrigeration to commercial-style ranges, we handle electrical upgrades, gas connections, and ventilation requirements.

From $3,000
Learn more
Pantry design & storage

Maximize every inch with smart pantry solutions. From walk-in pantries with custom shelving to butler’s pantries that streamline entertaining, we create organized storage that keeps ingredients accessible and kitchens clutter-free.

From $6,000
Learn more
Ventilation & hood systems

Keep your kitchen fresh and smoke-free with properly sized ventilation systems. We install range hoods from sleek under-cabinet units to statement chimney designs, with CFM ratings matched to your cooktop’s BTU output.

From $1,500
Learn more
Specialty stations

Elevate your kitchen with dedicated coffee and beverage stations, gourmet cooking stations with built-in wok burners or pizza ovens, and wine storage solutions. These specialty zones transform how you cook, entertain, and start your mornings.

From $4,000
Learn more
Michigan kitchen expertise
Kitchens designed for Michigan living

Michigan homes have unique demands that out-of-state designers miss. From humidity control to entertaining during Lions games, we understand how Southeast Michigan families actually use their kitchens.

Humidity-resistant materials

Michigan’s humid summers and dry winters wreak havoc on cheap materials. We select cabinets, countertops, and flooring rated for climate extremes, preventing warping, cracking, and premature wear.

Open-concept integration

Many Michigan homes feature cramped, closed-off kitchens. We safely remove load-bearing walls to create open layouts that connect kitchen, dining, and living spaces for modern entertaining.

Multi-county permit expertise

Kitchen remodels often require electrical, plumbing, and gas permits. We handle the paperwork across Washtenaw, Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Livingston, and Monroe counties so you don’t have to.

Local supplier relationships

Our partnerships with Michigan cabinet makers, countertop fabricators, and appliance dealers mean better selection, faster delivery, and priority service when you need warranty support.

Our process
From outdated to outstanding

Our design-build process eliminates the coordination chaos that makes traditional kitchen renovations stressful. One team, one contract, complete accountability.

1
Discovery call

We discuss your vision, cooking habits, and realistic budget expectations. You’ll know within this conversation if we’re the right fit for your kitchen project.

2
Kitchen assessment

Our team evaluates your current layout, measures every inch, and identifies plumbing and electrical requirements. We schedule your design consultation at your convenience.

3
Design & selections

Your project portal goes live with 3D visualizations, cabinet layouts, and material selections. You’ll see exactly what your kitchen will look like before we order a single cabinet.

4
Construction

Daily photos, weekly summaries, and instant access to your project manager. Our specialized crews handle demolition, rough-in, and finish work with minimal disruption to your daily life.

5
Final reveal

Detailed walkthrough, appliance training, and our satisfaction guarantee. We check in at 2 weeks, 1 month, and 3 months to ensure everything works perfectly.

Investment guide
Transparent pricing for kitchen remodels in Michigan

Every kitchen is unique, and final costs depend on size, layout changes, cabinet quality, countertop materials, and appliance selections. But we believe you deserve honest ranges before we ever schedule a consultation. These figures reflect actual 2024-2025 project costs in Southeast Michigan.

Unlike contractors who lowball estimates to win bids, then profit through change orders, our design consultation process produces a detailed, fixed-price proposal. What we quote is what you pay.

Need help financing your kitchen? Explore our financing options designed specifically for renovation projects, with competitive rates and flexible terms.

Common questions
Kitchen remodel FAQs

Planning a kitchen remodel raises important questions about costs, timelines, materials, and logistics. We’ve answered the most common questions here, but our team is always happy to discuss your specific situation.

Still have questions?

Every kitchen is unique. Schedule a consultation to discuss your specific remodel plans and get personalized answers.

Contact us
How much does a kitchen remodel cost in Michigan?
Kitchen remodel costs in Southeast Michigan typically range from $75,000 to $150,000+ for a complete renovation, depending on scope, materials, and layout changes. Custom cabinetry alone can range from $15,000 to $50,000, while premium countertops and backsplash typically run $5,000 to $20,000. We provide detailed, fixed-price proposals after our design consultation.
How long does a kitchen remodel take?
A complete kitchen remodel typically takes 6-10 weeks once construction begins. Simple cosmetic updates like new countertops and backsplash might take 2-3 weeks, while kitchens requiring layout changes, structural modifications, or new islands take longer. Our detailed project timeline is established before construction begins, with milestones tracked in your project portal.
Can I use my kitchen during remodeling?
For complete remodels, you won’t have a functional kitchen for several weeks. We help clients set up temporary kitchens with microwave, refrigerator, and hot plates in another room. Our dust containment systems with HEPA filtration keep construction debris from spreading throughout your home. Many clients find the temporary inconvenience well worth the final result.
Should I get stock, semi-custom, or custom cabinets?
Stock cabinets offer the fastest delivery and lowest cost but limited sizes and finishes. Semi-custom cabinets provide more options while remaining affordable. Custom cabinets are built to your exact specifications with unlimited finish and size options, plus premium features like soft-close hinges and dovetail joints. For most Southeast Michigan homeowners seeking lasting quality, we recommend semi-custom or custom cabinet solutions.
What countertop material is best for kitchens?
Quartz remains the most popular choice for its durability, low maintenance, and consistent appearance. Granite offers natural beauty and heat resistance. Marble provides timeless elegance but requires more maintenance. Butcher block adds warmth and can be refinished. During our design consultation, we discuss how each material performs for your cooking style and maintenance preferences.
Do I need permits for a kitchen remodel?
Permits are typically required when moving plumbing, adding electrical circuits, removing walls, or installing gas lines. Cosmetic updates like painting and cabinet replacement usually don’t require permits. Our team handles all permit applications, inspections, and code compliance across Washtenaw, Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Livingston, and Monroe counties. We ensure your kitchen meets all Michigan building codes.
What ROI can I expect from a kitchen remodel?
Kitchen remodels typically return 50-80% of their cost at resale, with minor refreshes often achieving higher percentages than gut renovations. But the real value is in daily enjoyment—a functional, beautiful kitchen transforms how you cook, entertain, and gather as a family. We help you balance investment with features that deliver both personal satisfaction and market appeal. Visit our portfolio to see completed projects.

Kitchen island

Make room for the room.

The one piece of a kitchen everyone ends up leaning on. Wright’s designs and builds kitchen islands for Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti homes, and every one of them starts with the three feet of floor around it.

Contact us now for a free quote
View our Portfolio

$4,000 to $15,000 for the island alone in Southeast Michigan. Price the whole kitchen

36in.
Walkway on every side. The minimum, not the goal.
42in.
On the seating side, counter edge to whatever is behind the stools.
12in.
Of overhang before stone needs hidden steel.
6by 3 ft
The island Wright’s builds most often in this region.
Clearance
It’s a game of inches.

An island is a clearance problem before it’s a design one. Thirty-six inches between the island and any counter, wall or appliance is the floor. Forty-two to forty-eight is what a two-cook kitchen wants. Forty-two on the seating side, and forty-eight if anyone will walk behind a seated guest. Most owners find on paper that the island needs to lose six inches, and finding that on paper costs nothing. The kitchen layout guide shows where an island fits in each plan.

Plan view, not to scale
36 in. min.
36 in. min.
42 in. seating side
48 in. if people pass behind
Size
How big, by how big the kitchen is.

Past about four feet deep nobody can reach the middle from either side, so the center becomes a place things go to be forgotten. Length follows the floor. The island sizing guide walks through the math room by room.

Under 120 sq ft
A prep island, if anything

A full island rarely fits once the clearances are honored. A narrow eighteen to twenty-four inch prep surface can, and so can a mobile island on casters. Small kitchen ideas cover the alternatives.

120 to 200 sq ft
Six by three

Four feet by two and a half gives you prep surface and storage. Six by three supports two stools plus a working zone, and it’s the island Wright’s builds most. Often it’s an island installation rather than a remodel.

Over 200 sq ft
Seven to ten feet

Three and a half to four feet deep, and long enough to carry a sink, seating and a working zone without crowding. Two counter runs of twenty-four inches plus a seam is the practical limit for the stone.

Seating
Pull up a stool. Mind the knees.

Counter height is thirty-six inches. Bar height is forty-two, paired with twenty-four-inch stools. Every seat wants twelve to fifteen inches of overhang, and anything past twelve inches in stone needs hidden steel, not faith. Decide early whether anyone in the house will sit there. Plenty of islands get seating nobody uses while the kitchen loses its floor to it. That conversation happens on the kitchen design side, before anything is ordered.

Stone
Twenty to thirty pounds a square foot.

A six-by-three top is carrying three hundred sixty to five hundred forty pounds, so the cabinet base under it is plywood and an overhang past twelve inches gets steel L-brackets set into the substrate. A stone cantilever with no steel cracks, usually at the seam, usually within two years. Quartz, granite or quartzite is the next decision, and the edge profile is the one after that.

Quartz, installed
$65 to $120 per sq ft
Granite
$60 to $100 per sq ft
Quartzite
$100 to $200 per sq ft
Marble
$120 to $250 per sq ft
Waterfall edge, both ends
$2,000 to $5,000
Water
Sink in the island, or against the window.

Against the window if you like looking outside while you work. In the island if you want to face the room. An island sink adds $2,000 to $3,500 for the drain and the vent, and it eats the largest continuous stretch of prep surface you have. Wright’s usually recommends a small, offset prep sink instead of the main one, with the countertop and backsplash planned around it.

A cooktop in the island works only when the island is long enough to keep forty-two inches on every working side, and you accept downdraft or a hood hanging mid-room. In most Michigan kitchens the range stays on the wall, and appliance installation gets simpler for it.

Light and power
Look up before you pick the pendants.

Is there a soffit or a duct where the pendants would hang, and can it move. Then look at the panel and count spare spaces. Code wants at least one GFCI outlet per four linear feet of countertop, and any built-in appliance in the island gets its own twenty-amp circuit. A second dishwasher or a wine unit is two circuits, not one. A new circuit runs $500 to $800 and a panel upgrade runs $2,000 to $4,000. The kitchen lighting page covers what hangs above once the ceiling is settled.

Storage
The half nobody plans.

Drawers beat doors inside an island. The practical set is a pair of pan drawers at twenty-four to thirty inches wide, a utensil drawer and a trash pull-out. Seating costs cabinetry: knees take that space, so a six-foot island with stools on one long side has about half the storage of one without. Custom cabinets make the most of what’s left, and a pantry nearby takes the overflow.

Michigan kitchens
The wall in the way.

The 1960s and 1970s ranches that fill Canton, Livonia and Novi were built with the kitchen boxed off, and those walls usually come out without drama. A non-load-bearing wall runs $1,000 to $3,000. A load-bearing one needs a beam and runs $3,000 to $8,000. In a 1925 bungalow the wall to the dining room is often load bearing, with plaster and a chase inside it, so Wright’s opens a small exploratory hole before quoting a beam. A guess there is a guess about several thousand dollars. Removing walls in older Michigan homes goes deeper.

Timeline
Two to three weeks, start to stone.

That’s for an island dropped into a kitchen that is otherwise finished. Water, power and walls each add time, and the Wright’s process sets the schedule before the first day.

Island only

A few days to set and level the base, template the top, then a week or so for the stone to be fabricated and installed.

Water or power

Add a week for electrical if new circuits have to be run, and two to three more if the island gets water and a drain.

A wall comes out

Plan on four to seven weeks and on losing the use of both rooms for part of it. Financing can spread the cost of the larger job.

Questions
Kitchen island questions, answered.
Can I add an island without a full remodel
How much does a kitchen island cost in Southeast Michigan
Is a kitchen island worth it at resale
What should I check before calling anyone
Ypsilanti, Michigan
Bring a tape measure and your floor plan.

Wright’s is a design-build contractor, so the person who draws the island is the one who answers for it on site. Clearances, stone, steel, circuits and the wall, settled in one plan.

Kitchen Countertop & Backsplash

Kitchen countertop and backsplash surfaces are the most visible, most touched, and most scrutinized elements in any kitchen remodeling project. They set the color palette, define the material character, and take daily abuse from hot pans, sharp knives, citrus acid, and red wine spills. Wright’s Renovations designs and installs countertop and backsplash combinations across Southeast Michigan that hold up to real life in a working kitchen, not just the first three months after installation.

The difference between a surface that ages well and one that chips, stains, or dates within a few years comes down to material selection, fabrication precision, and proper sealing. A quartz slab cut a quarter-inch short leaves a visible gap at the wall. A backsplash installed before the countertop sits creates a lipline that traps water and breeds mold. The sequencing and tolerances matter as much as the stone itself.

Why countertops and backsplashes anchor the entire kitchen design

Countertops and backsplashes occupy the largest uninterrupted visual plane in most kitchens. When someone walks into the room, these surfaces register before cabinetry finish details or hardware selections. They carry the color temperature of the space, establish whether the kitchen reads warm or cool, and determine how light reflects across the room throughout the day.

From a functional perspective, countertops bear the mechanical load of food preparation, small appliance staging, and casual dining. Backsplashes protect the drywall behind cooktops and sinks from grease, steam, and water. Neither surface is decorative alone. Both perform structural and protective roles that directly affect the longevity of the surrounding materials, including the plumbing fixtures seated into the countertop and the electrical outlets cut through the backsplash.

Wright’s Renovations treats these two surfaces as a single design decision, not two separate selections made in isolation. The team templates, fabricates, and installs countertops and backsplashes as a coordinated pair because seam lines, edge profiles, and grout color all interact. A mismatch between a polished countertop edge and a matte backsplash tile creates a visual tension that cheapens the entire kitchen, regardless of what either material cost on its own.

Countertop materials Wright’s Renovations installs across Southeast Michigan

Material selection is the highest-impact decision in any countertop project. Each stone, composite, or natural material carries different maintenance requirements, heat resistance, stain resistance, and cost profiles. Wright’s Renovations guides homeowners through these tradeoffs using actual material samples and finished project references, not just catalog photos.

Quartz countertops

Engineered quartz accounts for the majority of countertop installations Wright’s Renovations completes across Ann Arbor, Canton, and Plymouth. The material combines crushed natural quartz with polymer resins and pigments, producing a nonporous slab that resists staining without periodic sealing. Major manufacturers including Cambria, Caesarstone, and Silestone offer hundreds of colorways ranging from solid whites to veined patterns that closely replicate natural marble without the maintenance vulnerability.

Quartz handles daily kitchen abuse well. It resists scratches from normal use, does not absorb liquids, and cleans with soap and water. The surface cannot withstand direct heat above 300 degrees, so trivets remain necessary near cooktops. For homeowners who want the visual character of marble without the etching risk from lemon juice and tomato sauce, quartz with a soft-vein pattern is the most common recommendation from the Wright’s design team.

Granite countertops

Granite remains a strong choice for Birmingham and Northville homeowners who want the depth and movement of natural stone. Each slab is unique, with mineral deposits, veining patterns, and color variations that cannot be replicated in engineered materials. Granite is harder than quartz, handles direct heat without damage, and holds up to heavy use when properly sealed on an annual basis.

The tradeoff is maintenance. Granite is porous. Without regular sealing, it absorbs liquids and can develop dark spots around sink areas where standing water sits repeatedly. Wright’s Renovations applies commercial-grade penetrating sealers at installation and provides homeowners with specific resealing instructions for their particular stone grade. The team also helps clients navigate slab selection at local stone yards, where choosing the right cut from a specific block determines the final appearance.

Marble countertops

Marble is a premium surface that Wright’s Renovations installs selectively, typically in kitchens where the homeowner understands the material and accepts its maintenance demands. Marble etches on contact with acidic substances, scratches more easily than granite or quartz, and requires frequent sealing. It also develops a patina over time that some homeowners consider a feature and others consider damage.

Where marble appears most often in Wright’s projects is as a baking station insert or a kitchen island surface paired with quartz perimeter countertops. This approach gives the homeowner the visual impact of Calacatta or Carrara marble where they want it most, while protecting the high-traffic prep and cooking zones with a more forgiving material.

Butcher block and specialty surfaces

Solid wood countertops, particularly walnut and hard maple butcher block, appear in Wright’s projects as accent surfaces, island tops, or breakfast bar sections. Wood brings warmth and tactile variety to a kitchen dominated by stone and tile. It requires oiling every few months and can be sanded and refinished when scratched, which gives it a lifespan that rivals harder materials when properly maintained.

Specialty materials like soapstone, concrete, and recycled glass composites also appear in specific projects. Soapstone darkens naturally over time, developing a rich charcoal color that pairs well with traditional New England and farmhouse kitchen styles. Concrete allows custom coloring, integral drain boards, and unusual shapes, but requires professional sealing and can develop hairline cracks. Wright’s Renovations discusses these options during the kitchen design consultation so homeowners understand both the appeal and the realistic maintenance before committing.

Backsplash materials and design approaches for Michigan kitchens

The backsplash occupies the vertical space between countertop and upper cabinets, typically 15 to 18 inches in standard kitchen configurations. In kitchens with open shelving or no upper cabinets, backsplash tile can extend to the ceiling, creating a feature wall that transforms the entire room. Wright’s Renovations designs backsplash layouts that work with the countertop edge profile, cabinet color, and kitchen lighting placement as one integrated composition.

Ceramic and porcelain tile

Ceramic and porcelain tile offer the widest range of pattern, color, size, and price options for kitchen backsplashes. Subway tile in a 3-by-6-inch format remains the most requested backsplash in Wright’s kitchen projects, chosen for its clean lines and compatibility with both contemporary and traditional Canton and Plymouth kitchen styles.

Porcelain tile fires at higher temperatures than ceramic, producing a denser, more water-resistant product suited to the area directly behind sinks and cooktops where steam and splashing occur constantly. Large-format porcelain in 12-by-24-inch or 24-by-48-inch panels minimizes grout lines and creates a sleeker, more contemporary look. Wright’s Renovations installs large-format tile using a thin-set mortar system with leveling clips to ensure a flat, lippage-free surface across the entire backsplash run.

Glass tile and mosaics

Glass tile backsplashes reflect light differently than ceramic or stone, adding a luminous quality that changes throughout the day as natural light shifts. Mosaic sheets in 1-inch or 2-inch squares create intricate patterns with minimal grout lines, while linear glass tiles in stacked or offset layouts offer a modern geometric effect.

Installation requires specialized adhesive because glass is nonporous and does not bond to standard thin-set the way ceramic does. Wright’s Renovations uses white or light-colored adhesive behind glass tiles because dark adhesive shows through translucent material, altering the intended color. Grout selection also matters more with glass than with opaque tile, since the grout color becomes part of the visible design rather than just a filler.

Natural stone slab backsplashes

Full-slab backsplashes, cut from the same stone block as the countertop, create a continuous visual flow from the horizontal work surface up the wall. This approach eliminates grout lines entirely in the backsplash area and produces a dramatic, high-end look popular in Oakland County luxury kitchen renovations. Wright’s Renovations coordinates slab backsplash cuts during the countertop templating process to ensure veining patterns align across the L-shaped junction where the countertop meets the wall.

The cost of slab backsplashes runs higher than tile because the stone waste is greater and the installation requires precise cutting to work around outlets, switches, and window openings. However, for homeowners investing in premium stone or tile surfaces throughout their kitchen, a matched slab backsplash delivers visual continuity that tile cannot replicate.

Pairing countertops with backsplashes for a cohesive kitchen

The relationship between countertop and backsplash determines whether a kitchen reads as intentionally designed or accidentally assembled. Wright’s Renovations approaches the pairing as a single material decision by bringing physical samples of both surfaces together under the actual lighting conditions of the kitchen before any materials are ordered.

Contrast pairing places a bold backsplash against a neutral countertop, or vice versa. A white quartz countertop under a dark blue ceramic subway tile backsplash creates strong visual separation that defines the horizontal and vertical planes of the kitchen. This approach works well in smaller kitchens where the contrast adds perceived depth to the space.

Tone-on-tone pairing uses materials from the same color family at different textures or sheens. A honed marble countertop with a polished marble mosaic backsplash, both in warm grey tones, creates a layered, sophisticated look without competing patterns. This approach suits larger kitchens in Northville and Birmingham where the scale of the room supports subtlety over high contrast.

Wright’s Renovations also considers the relationship between surface materials and the surrounding elements: kitchen flooring, cabinet finish, appliance color, and natural light direction. A south-facing kitchen with warm afternoon light reads differently from a north-facing kitchen with cool, even light, and material colors shift accordingly. The team accounts for these environmental factors during material selection rather than discovering them after installation.

What countertop and backsplash projects cost in Southeast Michigan

Costs for countertop and backsplash work vary by material grade, linear footage, edge profile complexity, and the amount of demolition required to remove existing surfaces. The ranges below reflect actual project costs from Wright’s Renovations projects across Washtenaw County, Wayne County, and Oakland County.

Quartz countertops installed: $55 to $120 per square foot, depending on manufacturer, color, and edge profile. A typical 40-square-foot kitchen runs $2,200 to $4,800 for the countertop alone.
Granite countertops installed: $50 to $150 per square foot. Exotic granites with rare mineral patterns push toward the higher end, while common grades like Ubatuba or New Venetian Gold sit closer to $50.
Marble countertops installed: $75 to $200 per square foot. Calacatta Gold and Statuario command the highest prices due to limited quarry availability and veining consistency.
Tile backsplash installed: $15 to $40 per square foot for ceramic or porcelain. Glass and natural stone tile run $25 to $75 per square foot including labor.
Slab backsplash installed: $40 to $100 per square foot, cut and finished from the same stone as the countertop. This includes material, fabrication, and precision installation.

These prices include material, fabrication, delivery, installation, and sealing where applicable. They do not include demolition of existing countertops or any plumbing disconnection and reconnection required around sinks and dishwashers. Wright’s Renovations provides itemized pricing during the consultation process so homeowners see exactly where each dollar goes, with no hidden charges.

For homeowners planning a kitchen remodel in Birmingham or other Oakland County communities, countertop and backsplash selections typically represent 15% to 25% of the total kitchen renovation budget. Investing in durable, well-installed surfaces protects the rest of that budget by preventing water damage, staining, and premature replacement that cheap or poorly installed materials cause.

The installation process from template to finished surface

Countertop and backsplash installation follows a strict sequence that Wright’s Renovations has refined across hundreds of kitchen projects. Skipping steps or reversing the order creates fit problems that are expensive to fix after the fact. The process runs approximately two to three weeks from templating to final sealing, depending on material lead times and fabrication complexity.

Templating happens after cabinets are fully installed and leveled. A technician creates a precise digital or physical template of every countertop section, including sink cutouts, cooktop openings, outlet locations, and edge profile specifications. This template goes to the fabrication shop, where CNC machines or skilled stoneworkers cut the slabs to within one-sixteenth of an inch of the final dimensions.

Installation day begins with dry-fitting each countertop section to verify alignment and seam placement. The team applies adhesive, levels each section, and joins multi-piece countertops with color-matched epoxy that becomes invisible once cured. Sink and cooktop cutouts receive a polished edge treatment before plumbers and electricians return to make their final connections. The backsplash installation follows the countertop, using the finished countertop edge as the baseline reference for the first tile course.

Wright’s Renovations applies penetrating sealer to natural stone countertops and backsplashes immediately after installation, then allows 24 hours of cure time before the kitchen returns to active use. The team provides homeowners with a care guide specific to their installed materials, including recommended cleaning products, resealing intervals, and actions to avoid, such as placing hot pots directly on quartz surfaces or using acidic cleaners on marble or granite.

Michigan-specific considerations for kitchen surfaces

Southeast Michigan homes experience temperature swings of 100 degrees or more between winter lows and summer highs. This thermal cycling affects stone and tile materials differently than it affects homes in more temperate climates, particularly in kitchens with exterior walls where insulation quality varies by the age of the house.

Older homes in Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor built before the 1960s often have uninsulated or under-insulated exterior walls behind the kitchen backsplash zone. Cold wall temperatures in January can cause condensation behind tile that is not properly sealed, leading to mold growth invisible until the tile is removed. Wright’s Renovations inspects the wall assembly during demolition and addresses insulation or vapor barrier deficiencies before any new backsplash tile goes up.

Michigan water supplies also vary in mineral content by municipality. Hard water in communities served by well systems leaves calcium and lime deposits on stone surfaces over time. The team recommends specific stone sealers formulated for high-mineral-content water when the project location warrants it, rather than applying a generic sealer that may not hold up under local conditions.

Seasonal scheduling also factors into project planning. Countertop fabricators and tile suppliers in Southeast Michigan experience peak demand from May through October. Homeowners who finalize material selections during the winter months often receive faster fabrication turnaround and broader slab availability than those who begin the process in spring when every kitchen project in the region competes for the same production capacity.

How countertop and backsplash work connects to the full renovation

Surface installation rarely happens in isolation. Most Wright’s Renovations countertop and backsplash projects are part of a larger kitchen renovation that includes cabinetry, flooring, lighting, and plumbing work. The sequencing of trades matters because countertop templating cannot happen until cabinets are installed, backsplash tile cannot start until countertops are set, and final plumbing connections depend on both being complete.

For homeowners who are replacing countertops and backsplashes as a standalone update without a full kitchen gut, Wright’s Renovations coordinates the smaller scope with the same attention to sequencing. Existing countertop removal requires disconnecting sinks and cooktops, which means a licensed plumber and electrician participate even in surface-only projects. The team manages this coordination so the homeowner is not scheduling subcontractors independently.

Countertop and backsplash choices also influence adjacent renovation decisions. A thick, eased-edge granite countertop with a full backsplash tile run requires different cabinet depth and upper cabinet clearance than a thin quartz slab with a four-inch stone splash. Wright’s Renovations reviews these dimensional relationships early in the design process to prevent conflicts that show up at installation when it is too late to adjust.

Related kitchen services

Wright’s Renovations offers a full range of kitchen renovation services beyond countertop and backsplash installation. Many homeowners who begin with a surface upgrade expand their project to include related improvements that maximize the value of having a construction crew already on site.

Custom kitchen cabinetry provides the structural foundation that supports countertops, with options from stock to fully custom builds in any wood species and finish.
Walk-in pantry construction adds organized dry storage that frees countertop space for food preparation and cooking.
Bathroom renovation applies the same surface installation expertise to vanity countertops, shower tile, and tub surrounds.
Basement finishing extends the livable square footage of a home, often including a wet bar or kitchenette with its own countertop and backsplash surfaces.
Serving homeowners across Southeast Michigan

Wright’s Renovations installs kitchen countertops and backsplashes throughout six Southeast Michigan counties. The team serves homeowners in communities where kitchen surface materials need to perform in real Michigan conditions, from the high-humidity summers that test grout and sealant to the dry winters that stress adhesive bonds.

Schedule a kitchen surface consultation

The right countertop and backsplash combination starts with understanding how the kitchen is used, what maintenance commitment the homeowner is comfortable with, and how the surfaces relate to the rest of the room. Wright’s Renovations provides a detailed consultation that includes material samples, cost estimates, and a project timeline specific to the scope of work.

Call (734) 251-4187 or request a consultation online to discuss countertop and backsplash options for an upcoming kitchen project.

Kitchen flooring
Kitchen flooring has to survive a Michigan winter

Kitchen flooring takes more abuse than any other surface in the house. Dropped pans, a dishwasher that will eventually leak, salt tracked in from the driveway, and a humidity swing from about fifteen percent in a heated January house to over seventy percent in July. That swing is the Michigan variable, and it is why a floor that performs beautifully in Arizona cups here.

Installed market ranges in this region, by material. Luxury vinyl plank runs $5 to $10 per square foot, so $750 to $1,500 for a hundred and fifty square foot kitchen. Porcelain and ceramic tile run $8 to $18, or $1,200 to $2,700. Hardwood runs $11 to $21, or $1,650 to $3,150, split roughly $8 to $16 in material and $3 to $5 in labor. Natural stone runs higher: slate $10 to $20, travertine $10 to $22, limestone $12 to $25. Polishing an existing slab runs $4 to $8.

Two line items get left off most bids. Subfloor repair runs $2 to $6 per square foot when joists need leveling or a plywood overlay goes down, and self-leveling compound under tile adds $2 to $4. Neither is optional once the old floor comes up and the truth is visible. Our kitchen flooring options and costs piece has the material-by-material detail.

What each material is actually good at

Porcelain tile is the durability answer. Thirty years in, a good porcelain floor shows no worn paths and no discoloration, which almost nothing else can claim. Two conditions attach: it wants epoxy grout rather than cement grout, because cement grout needs annual sealing and will stain anyway, and it wants a flat substrate, which is where the self-leveling line item comes from.

Luxury vinyl plank is the value answer and it has earned its popularity. Waterproof, scratch resistant, unbothered by a dog or a leaking dishwasher, and the cheapest installed floor that does not look cheap. Its one real limitation is feel underfoot. It is a thin resilient layer over subfloor and it reads that way, which some people never notice and some notice immediately.

Hardwood is the aesthetic answer and the demanding one. In this climate it needs a minimum five-day acclimation in the room before installation, with a moisture meter reading rather than a calendar, or the boards will move seasonally and open gaps. It is worth doing when the kitchen is open to hardwood living space, because a material change at an open threshold is one of the most awkward lines in a house.

Stone is beautiful, cold, heavy and porous. It suits a specific house and a specific owner. Polished concrete over an existing slab is the cheapest floor on this page and the right answer more often than people expect, particularly in a walkout or a lower-level kitchen.

Heated floors, and which materials cooperate

Radiant heat under a kitchen floor runs $8 to $14 per square foot for materials and installation, which is $1,200 to $2,100 on a hundred and fifty square foot kitchen. It is the single upgrade our clients mention unprompted years later, and in a Michigan kitchen with a tile floor it changes whether anyone stands there barefoot in February.

Compatibility is not universal. Porcelain and ceramic are ideal, because tile conducts and does not care about the temperature. Hardwood works but has to run at a low temperature, with the surface capped around eighty-five degrees, and the species and construction both matter. Luxury vinyl plank varies by product and the manufacturer’s approval has to be confirmed in writing before the order goes in, not after. Our heated flooring page covers the systems and the controls.

The transitions nobody plans and everybody notices

A kitchen floor almost never stops at a wall. It meets hardwood in the dining room, carpet on a stair, tile in an entry and something else at the basement door. Those four lines are where a good floor either disappears into the house or announces that it was installed separately.

Height is the issue. Tile plus mortar plus backer board sits taller than luxury vinyl plank, so a tile kitchen next to an LVP hallway needs a reducer or a subfloor adjustment, and the adjustment looks better. Where the kitchen meets existing hardwood, running the same species and refinishing the whole floor at once is more expensive than a threshold and is the only version that actually looks like one house. In a mudroom or at a garage door, the change is welcome and should be deliberate rather than accidental.

The other transition worth planning is vertical. A floor that runs under the cabinets and under the appliances lets you change a dishwasher in ten years without a repair, and a floor that stops at the cabinet toe kick does not. It costs a little more square footage and saves a real problem.

What Michigan houses do to floors

In the 1920s bungalows and 1930s foursquares around Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti, the subfloor is usually diagonal board over joists that have settled, and the kitchen floor has been built up two or three times. Those floors are rarely flat, and the leveling work is the budget, not the tile. We check with a straightedge and a laser before quoting.

In the 1950s through 1980s houses across Plymouth, Canton and Livonia, the subfloor is plywood and generally sound, and the surprise is what is under the vinyl. Pre-1980 sheet vinyl and its adhesive can contain asbestos, so a test runs $200 to $400 and it happens before demolition rather than during. Any pre-1978 house also gets a lead paint test on trim before sanding.

Below grade, the concern shifts from wear to moisture. A slab moves vapor, so a lower-level kitchen wants a vapor barrier and a material that tolerates it. The same logic that governs basement flooring applies, and our basement flooring options piece covers the moisture testing.

What to look at before you spend anything

Set a marble on the floor in four places and watch what it does. Push a straightedge across the middle of the room and look for daylight under it. Open the dishwasher and look at the floor immediately in front of it for staining or soft spots, because that is where the leak already happened. Then check what the floor is at every doorway, and decide now whether you are matching, transitioning or replacing beyond the kitchen.

Then sequence it correctly. Flooring goes in after cabinets in some plans and before in others, and getting that order wrong costs either a repair or a floor under a cabinet you cannot service. Our kitchen remodel timeline lays out the sequence, and the mistakes to avoid covers what happens when it slips.

Questions we get asked
Can I put tile over my existing floor

Sometimes over a single layer of well-bonded vinyl, never over two or three layers, and never over a floor with any deflection. The saved demolition is small and the risk of a cracked floor is not. We look before answering.

Large format or small tile

Large format looks calmer and has fewer grout lines to clean, and it is far less forgiving of an uneven substrate. On an old bungalow floor a twelve by twenty-four tile will show every dip. Small format hides more and shows more grout.

What about the same floor through the whole first level

It is the best-looking answer and usually the right one in an open plan. It costs more than the kitchen alone, and it removes the transition problem entirely. Worth pricing both ways before deciding.

Will a new floor be enough on its own

If the cabinets are sound and the layout works, a floor is one of the highest-impact single changes in a kitchen. If the layout is the problem, a floor makes a bad layout look newer. The kitchen remodeling page is the honest starting point in that case.

Come stand on it with us

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, view our portfolio, or run numbers with the kitchen cost calculator. Surfaces that meet the floor are covered on countertops and backsplash and kitchen islands, and the full line-item picture is in our cost breakdown.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Bring us the straightedge result and we will tell you what the substrate is going to cost. Request an estimate to start, and see kitchen design for how selections work.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s kitchen flooring budget includes removal and disposal of the existing floor, subfloor inspection and repair, any self-leveling or plywood overlay the substrate needs, moisture testing where the floor sits on or below grade, the material, the underlayment or setting bed, installation, transitions at every doorway, quarter round or shoe as the trim detail requires, and daily photo updates.

It does not include appliances, moving your appliances back if a new floor changes the height under the dishwasher, asbestos or lead abatement if a test comes back positive, or repairs to joists we cannot see until the old floor is up. Any of those come to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect attached before work continues. If the floor turns out to be the least of the kitchen’s problems, the cabinetry and lighting conversations are the honest next ones, and renovation financing is what makes the larger scope reachable.

How long it takes and where you eat

Luxury vinyl plank in a typical kitchen goes down in two to three days. Tile runs four to seven days, because mortar and grout each need to cure and neither can be rushed. Hardwood runs five to eight days including the acclimation period, and site-finished hardwood adds two to four more for sanding and coats. Add one to three days at the front if the subfloor needs work, which is the most common schedule variable.

You lose the kitchen floor, which in practice means you lose the kitchen. Plan on a temporary setup somewhere else in the house for the duration: a microwave, a kettle, the coffee maker and a folding table. Tile is the hardest stretch because you cannot walk on it between the set and the grout, so we tape off a route and tell you which two days are the strict ones. Site-finished hardwood is the other one to plan around, since the finish needs the room empty and ventilated.

Interior flooring runs year round here with no weather constraint, which is why our winter calendar fills with it. One caveat on materials in January: anything delivered off a cold truck needs time in the room before it goes down, and hardwood needs the full acclimation period measured with a meter rather than a calendar. Rushing that in February is how a floor that looked perfect in March opens gaps in July. If the floor is going in as part of a larger remodel, it gets sequenced against the cabinets rather than scheduled on its own.
