Kitchen lighting
Kitchen lighting is three systems, and most kitchens have one

Most Michigan kitchens we walk into have a single fixture in the middle of the ceiling. It puts your own shadow on the counter you are working at, it makes the cabinets look flat, and from November to February it is doing the whole job, because the sun sets before quarter past five in December here.

Good kitchen lighting is three separate layers on three separate switches. Ambient light fills the room. Task light lands on the counters, the sink and the range where the work happens. Accent light does the cabinets, the backsplash and the island, and it is the layer that makes a kitchen look designed rather than lit.

Market ranges in this region, by piece. Six to ten recessed cans run $1,200 to $2,500 installed. Under-cabinet LED runs $800 to $1,500. Pendants over an island run $400 to $2,000 depending on the fixtures. A new circuit runs $500 to $800, and a panel upgrade runs $2,000 to $4,000. Outlet and USB upgrades run $100 to $200 per location. A full kitchen electrical budget lands at $4,000 to $8,000, and our kitchen line-item breakdown shows where that sits against everything else.

The numbers that make it look right

Color temperature is the setting people get wrong most often. Kitchens want 2700K to 3000K, which reads as warm white. Anything at 4000K or above turns a kitchen clinical, makes wood cabinets look grey and makes food look wrong, and it is what big-box fixtures default to. Ask for the number, not the word on the box.

Color rendering matters almost as much and nobody mentions it. A CRI of ninety or better is what lets you see whether the chicken is done and whether the paint sample actually matches. Cheap LED runs at eighty and it is visible in a kitchen even if you cannot name what is off.

Then placement. Under-cabinet strips go toward the front edge of the cabinet bottom, not the back, or the light hits the backsplash and glares back at you instead of landing on the counter. Recessed cans go over the front edge of the counter rather than centered in the ceiling, so you are not standing between the light and your work. Pendants over an island hang with about thirty to thirty-six inches between the counter and the bottom of the fixture, and they get spaced off the island ends rather than the room walls.

Everything gets dimmed. A kitchen at full output is right for chopping and wrong for every other hour, and dimming is the cheapest quality-of-life item on this page. Smart controls extend that to scenes and schedules, and our specialty lighting design page covers the more ambitious versions.

Code, circuits and the panel

Kitchen electrical is one of the more heavily governed parts of a house, for good reason. Countertop receptacles are GFCI protected. Code wants at least one outlet per four linear feet of countertop, and any built-in appliance gets its own twenty-amp circuit. Adding lighting layers frequently means adding circuits, and adding circuits means the panel needs spare spaces.

That is where older houses get expensive. A 1950s hundred-amp panel that is already full turns a lighting project into a service conversation, and the panel upgrade is $2,000 to $4,000 before a single fixture goes in. We count the spaces on the first visit rather than discovering it at rough-in. Our overview of Michigan kitchen codes and licensing covers what gets inspected and when.

One more Michigan-specific item. In houses built before about 1950, particularly around Ypsilanti and older Ann Arbor neighborhoods, knob-and-tube wiring still turns up in kitchen ceilings. It cannot be extended and it cannot be buried in insulation, so any lighting plan in those houses starts with what gets replaced rather than what gets added.

Plaster ceilings and the recessed can problem

In drywall, a recessed light is a hole saw and a remodel can with spring clips. In plaster over wood lath, it is a different job. The lath resists a hole saw, the plaster keys break away from the lath around the cut, and a can that clips to plaster alone will eventually sag. It is doable, it is slower, and it needs patching by someone who can match a plaster ceiling.

Which is why the honest recommendation in an older house is sometimes not recessed lighting at all. Surface-mounted fixtures, track discreetly placed, a larger central fixture doing ambient work with the task layer under the cabinets, and pendants where the plan wants a moment. That combination reads better in a 1925 kitchen than a grid of cans, and it costs less.

If the ceiling is coming down anyway for other reasons, the calculation flips entirely and recessed becomes cheap. That is worth knowing before the demolition scope is set, which is a design conversation rather than an electrical one. The kitchen design page covers how those two get sequenced.

What each surface needs

Five decisions cover almost every kitchen we light.

Counters get under-cabinet light on every run where anyone works, on its own switch, dimmable, warm.
The sink gets a dedicated fixture or a can directly above it, because dishes at night are the most common task in the room.
The range gets light in the hood, and the hood light gets checked for output, since most builder hoods are useless.
The island gets pendants for the look and a can or two for the work, since pendants alone leave the far edge dark.
Inside glass cabinets and in a walk-in pantry gets light on a door switch, which is a small cost and a daily pleasure.

Toe-kick lighting is the optional one worth mentioning. It costs little during a remodel, it gives you a kitchen you can walk into at two in the morning without waking the house, and it cannot be added later without pulling cabinets.

What to look at before you spend anything

Stand at your main prep counter in the evening with the lights on and look at whether your own shadow is on the cutting board. That single observation tells you whether you need task lighting or a new ceiling fixture, and they are different projects. Then check the color temperature printed on your existing bulbs. Then open the panel and count blank spaces. Then look at whether the ceiling is drywall or plaster, which you can usually tell by tapping it.

After that it is selections, and lighting is the one category where the fixtures should be chosen against the cabinet and countertop finishes rather than on their own. See custom cabinets and countertops and backsplash, because a warm brass pendant against a cool grey quartz is a decision, not an accident. The mistakes to avoid piece covers the ones we see repeated.

Questions we get asked
How many recessed cans does a kitchen need

Fewer than most plans show. Six to ten covers most kitchens we work in, placed over work surfaces rather than spaced evenly across the ceiling. A ceiling full of cans lights the floor beautifully and the counters poorly.

Are LED strips under cabinets worth it

They are the highest-value item on this page at $800 to $1,500. Specify a continuous linear fixture rather than puck lights, or you get scallops of light and dark along the counter, which is the look people are trying to avoid.

Can lighting be updated without a remodel

Yes, and it is one of the few kitchen improvements that stands alone well. Under-cabinet light, better bulbs at the right temperature, dimmers and one good fixture over the sink is a one to two day job with real daily payoff.

What about natural light

Worth chasing before you add fixtures. A larger window or a skylight changes a north-facing kitchen more than any lamp will, and it belongs in the design conversation with the rest of the kitchen remodel.

Turn the lights on with us standing there

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits, the electrical and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, or view our portfolio. Lighting elsewhere in the house is covered on basement lighting, in our basement lighting guide, on bathroom lighting and ventilation and on outdoor lighting.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. We will come at dusk if you want to see the difference rather than hear about it. Request an estimate to start, and the kitchen flooring and island pages cover what the light lands on.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s kitchen lighting budget includes the lighting plan itself, permits and electrical inspection, new circuits and any panel work the plan requires, recessed housings and trims, under-cabinet fixtures and their drivers, pendant fixtures and boxes rated for them, switching and dimmers, GFCI protection at the countertops, drywall or plaster patching where fixtures go in, paint touch-up on the affected surfaces, and daily photo updates.

It does not include decorative fixtures you buy elsewhere and hand us, though we are glad to install them and will tell you honestly whether a fixture will do the job it is being asked to do. It also excludes knob-and-tube replacement beyond the work area, a service upgrade if the utility requires a new drop, and repairs to conditions found once a ceiling is opened. Those come to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect before work continues.

How long it takes

Under-cabinet lighting alone is a one to two day job in a finished kitchen. A full lighting plan with recessed cans, pendants and new switching runs five to ten working days in drywall, spread across rough-in, inspection, patching, paint and trim-out. Plaster ceilings add two to four days for the patching and the plaster to cure before paint.

A panel upgrade is its own event. It means a scheduled power shutdown, a utility coordination window, and an inspection, and it typically adds three to five days to the front of the project. We would rather tell you that in the first meeting than at rough-in, which is why the panel gets counted on the first visit.

One sequencing note. Lighting rough-in has to happen before drywall and before cabinets go on the wall, because a fixture location that moves after the boxes are set means patching finished surfaces. If the plan is a staged remodel, the lighting layout gets decided in the first stage even when the fixtures get installed in the last one.

The disruption is modest compared with most kitchen work. Power goes off in scheduled windows rather than for days, the sink and the range stay usable, and the dusty part is the patching. If lighting is going in alongside a larger remodel it gets sequenced with the rest, and the kitchen remodel timeline shows where it lands. Renovation financing covers the larger version.

Kitchen pantry
A kitchen pantry is the cheapest storage in the house

A kitchen pantry is the least expensive square footage in a renovation and the one people notice most in daily use. Nothing else in a kitchen budget delivers as much for as little, because a pantry is framing, shelving, a door and a light. No plumbing, no stone, no appliances.

Market ranges run $250 to $5,000 with an average near $2,000. A reach-in runs $250 to $1,500. A small walk-in runs $750 to $2,000. A large walk-in runs $2,000 to $3,500. Per square foot that is $20 to $40 for a standard build, and $50 to $450 per linear foot at the custom end where cabinetry replaces shelving.

The pieces price out simply. Plywood or wire shelving runs $400 to $750. Stock cabinets run $100 to $300 per linear foot installed. A light fixture runs $160 to $1,000. Taking out a wall runs $300 to $1,000. An electrician runs $6 to $8 per square foot, and a cabinet maker runs $35 to $100 an hour. Permits, where a wall moves, run $400 to $2,200. Those are market figures rather than a quote.

Three kinds of pantry, and which one you have room for

A reach-in is a closet with good shelves, about five feet wide and two feet deep. You stand outside it and everything is visible at once, which is the underrated advantage. It fits in a wall recess, an old broom closet or the end of a cabinet run, and it is the right answer far more often than people expect.

A walk-in starts around five feet by five feet. You get more volume and more wall, and you lose the see-everything-at-once quality unless the lighting is right. Below about five feet square a walk-in stops working, because you cannot open a door, stand inside and still reach the shelves behind the door swing.

A butler’s pantry is a different thing entirely. It is a working room between the kitchen and the dining room with counter, storage and often a sink, and it belongs in a house that entertains. It is closer in cost and complexity to a small kitchen than to a pantry, and the two get conflated in listings constantly.

Shelf depth is the dimension that decides whether any of them works. Twelve inches is right. Eighteen is the maximum for a larger space, and anything deeper becomes a place where cans go to expire behind other cans. Two shallow walls beat one deep one every time.

The Michigan houses that have no pantry at all

The 1950s through 1970s ranches and colonials across Canton, Livonia, Westland and Novi were built with a single narrow broom closet and nothing else. Those kitchens were designed around a weekly grocery trip and a much smaller inventory of packaged food than any household keeps now, and the storage gap is the most common complaint we hear about them.

The bungalows and foursquares around Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti usually had a real pantry originally, often with a window, and it was absorbed into a 1980s remodel to make the kitchen feel bigger. Finding it is frequently a matter of looking at where the plaster changes and where an odd bulkhead runs, and reclaiming that space is cheaper than building new.

And there is a regional habit that matters. Bulk shopping is normal here, which means the storage requirement is not cans and boxes but paper goods, cases of water and a chest freezer’s worth of overflow. A pantry sized for a tidy magazine photo will not hold a Costco run, and pretending otherwise is how the garage becomes the pantry by February. We size for what people actually buy.

Where it should go

Close to where groceries come in beats close to the stove. The walk from car to counter to shelf is the trip you make every week, and a pantry on the far side of the kitchen from the entry door means every bag crosses the working triangle. If the entry is through a mudroom or a garage door, the pantry wants to be within a few steps of it.

Five places we find the space, in rough order of cost. An existing coat or broom closet backing onto the kitchen. A section of an oversized adjacent room, often a dining room that is larger than anyone uses. The end of a cabinet run converted from base cabinets to a full-height unit. A stolen three or four feet from an attached garage. And a bump-out, which is the most expensive and the only one that adds floor area to the house.

What almost never works is the basement. Storage down a flight of stairs is storage nobody uses for daily cooking, and it turns into long-term overflow instead. That has its own value and it belongs under basement storage systems rather than being called a pantry.

What separates a good one from a closet with shelves

Five details, and none of them costs much during construction.

Light on a door switch, so it comes on when you open it. A dark pantry gets used at half capacity because you cannot read a label at the back.
Adjustable shelving, because the height a cereal box needs and the height a stand mixer needs are not the same and will change.
One deep low shelf or open floor for cases, bulk paper goods and the things too heavy to lift to eye level.
A counter surface in a walk-in, even eighteen inches of it, which becomes where the small appliances live plugged in and out of sight.
An outlet, for that counter and for a charging shelf, which is a five-minute addition at rough-in and impossible afterward.

Doors matter more than they seem. A hinged door needs swing clearance in a kitchen that has none to spare, a pocket door solves that and costs more in framing, and a barn-style slider is the cheapest solution to the same problem. Wide and shallow beats tall and narrow, because a two-foot door on a five-foot pantry hides half of it.

Cabinetry versus shelving is the real cost fork. A pantry fitted out in custom cabinets or custom millwork looks superb and costs several times a well-built shelving system. Our guide to stock, semi-custom and custom cabinets covers where that money goes.

What to look at before you spend anything

Empty your current food storage onto the counter and look at it. That pile is your actual requirement, and it is almost always taller and heavier than the pantry people ask for. Then walk the route from your car to where the food ends up and count the steps. Then tap the walls around the kitchen and find out which ones are hollow, because a wall with nothing in it is the cheapest place to put a reach-in.

Then check the boring constraint. Is there ductwork, a stack or old wiring in the wall you want to open, and is the wall bearing. That answer moves a pantry from $1,000 to $4,000 and it is worth knowing on day one. If the kitchen is small and every option is tight, our small kitchen ideas and kitchen layout types pieces cover the trades plainly.

Questions we get asked
Does a pantry add value at resale

A custom pantry returns fifty to seventy-five percent, which is strong for a storage improvement, and buyers in this region read a real pantry as a sign the kitchen was thought about. It is also one of the few items that shows well in photos without a stylist.

Reach-in or walk-in if I can have either

Reach-in, in most kitchens under about two hundred square feet. You see everything, you lose no floor to circulation inside it, and the money goes into shelving rather than into a room. Walk-in wins when the volume really requires it or when a counter inside earns its keep.

Can I add one without touching the kitchen

Frequently yes. Converting a closet or a cabinet run is a two to four day job with no plumbing and often no permit. It is one of the few things on our site that really is a small project.

What about a coffee station in there

Popular and worth doing, and it needs an outlet and ideally that counter. If it is going to be a real fixture of the morning, a purpose-built coffee and beverage station outside the pantry keeps traffic out of the food storage. Serious cooks tend the same way about a gourmet cooking station.

Empty the cupboards, then call us

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, or view our portfolio. The rest of the kitchen is covered on kitchen remodeling, islands, lighting and kitchen design.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Show us the pile on the counter and we will size the shelves to it. Request an estimate to get on the calendar.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s pantry budget includes the design, any permit and inspection where a wall moves, framing, drywall and paint, the door and its hardware, shelving or cabinetry as specified, lighting with a door switch, an outlet where the plan calls for one, trim to match the rest of the room, and daily photo updates.

It does not include relocating a stack, a duct or a panel found inside the wall we open, and it does not include flooring beyond the pantry footprint unless the room is getting a new floor anyway. Where continuing the kitchen material into the pantry is the better-looking answer, that gets priced with the kitchen flooring rather than hidden here. Anything found behind the plaster comes to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect attached.

How long it takes

Converting an existing closet runs two to four days. Building a reach-in into a hollow wall runs four to seven. A walk-in that takes space from an adjacent room runs one to two weeks including paint. Add cabinet lead time if the fit-out is millwork rather than shelving, which is usually four to eight weeks from order and is the item that sets the schedule.

Disruption is the mildest of anything on our site. You keep your kitchen, your water and your appliances. What you lose is the wall the work is happening on and a few days of dust. Interior work like this runs through a Michigan winter without a weather delay, which makes a pantry a good January project and a good way to use the gap while cabinets for a larger job are being built. One thing worth deciding early is whether the pantry shares the kitchen’s finish schedule. Matching paint, trim profile and hardware to the kitchen makes the pantry read as part of the room, and it costs nothing extra if it is specified at the same time rather than six months later from a different can. The kitchen remodel timeline shows how it fits alongside the rest, and renovation financing covers the bigger scope.

Bathroom remodeling · Southeast Michigan
Bathroom remodeling in Southeast Michigan

A bathroom remodel is the renovation where small mistakes get expensive. Water finds every gap a crew leaves behind, and a shower built a quarter inch out of level shows for the life of the house. Wright’s Renovations builds bathrooms as a design-build firm, so the people who draw the tile layout are the same people who set it. One team, one contract, one number to call across Washtenaw, Wayne, and Oakland County.

The case for one team
Why a wet room punishes shortcuts

A kitchen forgives a lot. A bathroom forgives almost nothing. The room runs on water under pressure, a drain that has to pitch correctly toward the trap, and a tile surface that reads every flaw under hard overhead light. The expensive failures are the invisible ones: a membrane lapped the wrong way, a pan that never got pressure tested, a valve set too deep for the trim to seat. None of that shows on the day the job wraps. It shows two winters later.

When the people who design the layout hand it to a separate crew, the seams between trades become the seams where water gets in. Wright’s Renovations runs the work as one bathroom renovation team, so the layout, the waterproofing plan, and the install belong to the same group of people. The plumber knows where the designer put the niche before the wall is open, and the tile setter knows the slope before the mortar goes down.

That single line of accountability is the point of the design-build model. There is no finger pointing between a designer and a builder who never met, because the homeowner signs one contract for both. The estimate is itemized to the dollar before anyone swings a hammer, and the price holds when the drywall comes off and the real condition of the old plumbing finally shows itself.

The part nobody sees
Waterproofing first, tile second

Tile and grout are not the water barrier. The barrier is the bonded membrane behind them, and it is the single detail that decides whether a shower lasts five years or twenty-five. Wright’s crews run a continuous membrane across every wet wall, lap it correctly down into the pan, and bond it to the drain flange so water that gets behind the tile still has nowhere to go but down the drain. Inside corners and the curb get a second layer, because that is where movement cracks a rigid surface.

The shower floor is built on a pre-slope that pitches a consistent quarter inch per foot toward the drain, so water never pools under the tile. Before a single piece of tile is set, the pan gets flood tested and held overnight. A pan that holds water for hours dry is a pan that will hold up for the life of the full bathroom remodel.

Tile alignment is the visible half of the same discipline. The layout starts from the wall the eye lands on, not from a random corner, so grout lines run continuous from the shower floor up the wall and straight into the recessed niche. The niche sits on a tile course instead of cutting through one. Large-format tile gets lippage control so no edge stands proud of its neighbor, and the result reads as one surface rather than a field of patched squares.

A bonded membrane behind every wet wall, lapped into the pan
A pre-sloped, flood-tested shower pan held overnight before tile
Grout lines aligned from the shower floor across the niche
Sealed penetrations at the valve, the spout, and the drain flange
Lippage control on large-format tile so edges sit flush
Where the budget actually goes

Most of the cost of a bathroom lives behind the finishes. Demolition exposes the old condition of the framing, the supply lines, and the subfloor, and the honest version of a bathroom budget plans for that before the wall comes off rather than after.

A working bathroom in a tight footprint asks different questions than a large suite. The team handles both, and a small bathroom remodel often gains the most from a smarter layout rather than a bigger one. Finished baths show the range: green tile and brass in Dexter, a floating vanity in Livonia, and two baths built together in Ann Arbor.

Daily use
Vanity, storage, and what you reach for

A bathroom earns its keep at the vanity, where the storage either fits the way a household actually gets ready or fights it every morning. Drawers beat doors for almost everything a person reaches for at the sink, because a drawer brings the back of the cabinet to the front instead of hiding it behind a hinge. Wright’s plans the cabinet around what goes in it, then sizes the drawers to match.

An outlet inside the vanity keeps a hair dryer and a toothbrush charger off the counter and out of sight. A tall linen run, where the floor plan has room, takes towels out of the hall closet. In a compact room, a wall-hung vanity shows more floor and reads larger, which is why it appears in so much of the company’s bathroom design work for older Southeast Michigan homes with small original baths.

Lighting belongs at face height, not only on the ceiling, so the mirror does not throw shadows under the eyes. The vanity height gets set to the people who use it rather than to a builder default. These are small decisions, and they are the ones a homeowner notices every single day for the next twenty years.

Soft-close drawers sized for what they actually hold
An outlet inside the cabinet to clear the counter
A tall linen run wherever the plan allows it
Lighting at face height alongside the overhead fixture
Vanity height set to the household, not a default
Fixtures and water
Fixtures and water that does not fight you

The fixture a homeowner picks for its looks is only half the decision. The valve behind it decides whether the shower scalds when a toilet flushes somewhere else in the house. Wright’s specifies pressure-balancing or thermostatic valves so the water holds its temperature when demand changes, and sets them at the right depth for the trim to seat clean against the finished tile.

Moisture is the enemy of every new finish in the room, so the exhaust fan gets sized to the square footage and vented to the outside, not into the attic. A fan that runs a few minutes after the shower pulls the humidity out before it settles into the grout and the paint. Skipping that step is how a remodel that looked perfect on day one grows mildew along the ceiling by spring.

Water efficiency does not have to mean a weak shower. Modern low-flow showerheads and dual-flush or high-efficiency toilets hold their performance while using less, which matters on a Southeast Michigan water bill and matters more if the home runs on a well and septic field. Finishes get chosen with local water in mind, because hard water spots some platings faster than others. A bathroom that pairs with a kitchen remodel can share the same fixture line for a consistent look through the main floor.

A pressure-balancing or thermostatic valve so the temperature holds
An exhaust fan sized to the room and vented outside
Efficient fixtures that keep pressure while using less water
Finishes chosen to stand up to local hard water
A layout that keeps the toilet out of the sightline from the door
A bathroom rarely travels alone

A primary bath often gets built alongside a larger project, and the planning is cleaner when the trades are scheduled together. A finished lower level usually wants a bathroom of its own, which the team folds into the same plan during basement remodeling.

If the house simply needs one more bathroom rather than a redo of an existing one, the plumbing and framing questions change, and adding a bathroom is its own service with its own approach.

How the work runs
How a Wright’s bathroom gets built

Every project follows the same shape, scaled to fit the room. A homeowner always knows what week the job is in, what comes next, and what it costs.

01
The consultation

A free 60 to 90 minute conversation in the home. Connor Wright walks the space, listens to the goal, and gives a straight read on what is feasible at what budget.

02
The plan and the number

Designers and project managers build out the scope, the materials, and the schedule. The estimate is itemized to the dollar, with a five-payment schedule tied to real milestones.

03
The build

One crew, not a rotation of random subs. Daily photos and a Friday recap post to JobTread, the same project view the manager sees, with change orders signed digitally.

04
The walkthrough

The team walks the finished room, punches out anything imperfect, fixes it, and hands over a five-year craftsmanship warranty, with check-ins at two weeks, one month, and three months.

Service area
Bathrooms across Southeast Michigan

From the company’s headquarters in Ypsilanti, Wright’s builds bathrooms across six counties, and the older housing stock in the region keeps the work interesting. A 1920s home in Ann Arbor hides different surprises behind the plaster than a mid-century ranch in Oakland County or newer construction out in Livingston County, and the design-build approach absorbs those surprises without a change-order fight.

Homeowners in higher-end markets tend to look for a contractor who treats a bathroom like the precise wet-space build it is. The team handles those projects directly, including Birmingham bathroom remodeling in Oakland County and detailed work for Rochester Hills homeowners who expect the tile to be perfect. The full Michigan service area reaches well beyond those two communities.

Common questions about bathroom remodeling
How long does a bathroom remodel take?

It depends on the scope, and the honest answer comes during design rather than over the phone. A finish-level refresh moves faster than a full gut that opens the walls and reworks the plumbing. Once the scope is set, the schedule goes into the contract with a real timeline, and the homeowner tracks progress daily through the JobTread portal.

Bathroom lighting and ventilation
The cheapest thing in your bathroom protects everything else in it

Bathroom lighting and ventilation is where a few hundred dollars decides whether a twenty-five thousand dollar bathroom lasts. A complete exhaust system, properly sized and properly ducted, runs $370 to $1,050 installed. Mold remediation runs $2,000 to $6,000. Framing repair from chronic moisture runs $3,000 to $8,000. Ceiling and paint repair below a leaking bathroom runs $500 to $1,500.

That is the entire argument, and it is why we will not build a bathroom around a builder-grade fan. The itemized version: a quality low-noise fan unit runs $120 to $300, insulated ductwork $100 to $300, the exterior termination cap $50 to $150 plus $100 to $250 to install it, and the electrical connection and switch $100 to $200 basic or $150 to $300 with a timer or humidity sensor.

Lighting runs alongside it and is the other half of why a bathroom either feels finished or feels like a builder left. Those are market figures rather than a quote.

How big the fan has to be

Michigan code sets fifty cubic feet per minute as the floor for a bathroom under a hundred square feet. That is a minimum, not a target, and it is why so many bathrooms have a fan that technically complies and does nothing.

The working rule is one CFM per square foot of floor area. A sixty-square-foot bathroom wants sixty CFM. A room with a steam shower or a large soaking tub wants one and a half CFM per square foot, because there is far more moisture to move. Then add ten to twenty percent on top of whatever that calculation gives you, to cover the airflow you lose to the ductwork between the fan and the outside.

Noise is the specification that decides whether the fan gets used, and it is measured in sones. One sone is barely audible. Three sones is conversation-level background noise. Above four sones is loud enough that people stop turning it on, which makes the whole system worthless. We specify in the 0.3 to 1.0 sone range at eighty to a hundred and fifty CFM, and the difference between that and a big-box fan is about a hundred and fifty dollars.

Our writeup on bathroom ventilation in Michigan works through the sizing with examples, and the numbers behind it sit in the Southeast Michigan cost breakdown.

The duct is where most installations fail

A perfect fan on bad ductwork moves almost no air. Four rules cover it.

The duct diameter matches the fan outlet. A four-inch fan gets four-inch duct, a six-inch fan gets six-inch duct, and necking a six down to a four to reuse an old run wastes the fan you just paid for. The material is rigid metal or insulated flexible duct rated for the job. Standard dryer vent hose has too much internal resistance and is the single most common thing we find in older installations.

Every ninety-degree elbow costs roughly fifteen feet of equivalent duct length in airflow. That means a fan ten feet from the exterior with four elbows in the run is performing as though it were seventy feet away. Straighter is dramatically better, and it is worth moving the fan location during design to get it.

Where the duct crosses an unconditioned attic or crawl space it gets R-6 or R-8 insulation. An uninsulated duct in a near-zero-degree Michigan attic condenses on the inside, the water runs back down and drips through the fan housing into your ceiling, and the homeowner reasonably concludes the roof is leaking. And the duct terminates at a roof cap or a sidewall cap. Venting into the attic is a Michigan building code violation and the most expensive shortcut in this trade.

Controls, because a fan you have to remember is a fan you forget

Moisture needs about twenty minutes of exhaust after a shower to clear. Nobody stands in a bathroom for twenty minutes after they leave it, which is why a plain wall switch is the weakest link in an otherwise good system.

A timer switch costs $25 to $60 for the switch plus $50 to $100 to install, and it runs the fan for a set period after you walk out. A humidity sensor costs $80 to $150 and does better: it starts the fan when relative humidity climbs past around sixty percent and stops when the room is dry, whether anyone touched a switch or not. In a bathroom used by kids or guests, the sensor is the version that actually works.

One control note for a steam room. The exhaust runs after the session rather than during it, so the switching gets designed alongside the generator controls rather than bolted on.

Lighting in three layers

Most bathrooms have one fixture over the mirror or one in the middle of the ceiling, and both put your own shadow exactly where you need to see. Good bathroom lighting is three jobs on separate switches.

Ambient light fills the room and can come from a ceiling fixture or from recessed cans placed toward the walls rather than dead center. Task light is the one that matters at the mirror, and it wants to come from the sides at roughly eye level, flanking the mirror, rather than from above. Sconces or vertical fixtures at about sixty-five inches off the floor light a face evenly. A single bar above the mirror puts shadows under the eyes and the nose, which is why bathroom mirrors so often feel unflattering.

Accent light does the shower, a niche, a tub alcove or a toe kick. Anything inside a shower or above a tub needs a damp-rated or wet-rated fixture, which is a code requirement rather than a preference. And every layer gets a dimmer, because the light level you want at seven in the morning is not the level you want at two.

Specify 2700K to 3000K for warm white and a color rendering index of ninety or better. Below ninety, makeup and paint colors read wrong and you will not be able to say why. Bigger schemes are covered on specialty lighting design, and smart controls add scenes and schedules.

What Michigan does to a bathroom

Two climate facts drive the whole specification. In January the difference between the inside of your bathroom and the outside face of an exterior wall regularly exceeds seventy degrees, and that gradient condenses moisture on cold surfaces whether anyone showered or not. In July outdoor humidity runs above seventy percent, and indoor levels sit at fifty-five to sixty-five even with air conditioning running.

Mold becomes active above eighty percent relative humidity. A bathroom with a fifty-CFM fan and a long flexible duct hits that every day it gets used, and the first evidence is dark grout in the corners and paint peeling at the ceiling line. Neither is a tile problem or a paint problem.

Older housing stock adds a wrinkle. In pre-1950 houses around Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor there is often no bathroom fan at all, because the original design relied on an operable window. A window is not ventilation in February, when nobody opens it. Those bathrooms need a fan run added, and the routing is the design problem: through a plaster ceiling to a roof cap, or through the rim joist to a sidewall cap on a first-floor bath.

What to look at before you spend anything

Five checks, all free.

Hold a square of tissue to the fan grille while it runs. If it does not hold, the fan is not moving meaningful air.
Go into the attic and find where the duct ends. If it ends in the attic, that is the whole problem and it is a code violation.
Count the bends in the duct run, because each ninety costs about fifteen feet of performance.
Look at the grout in the shower corners and the paint at the ceiling line, which is where inadequate exhaust shows first.
Stand at the mirror and look at where the light comes from. If it is only overhead, the task layer is missing.

Then check the switch. A single switch running both the light and the fan means the fan only runs while someone is in the room, which is exactly backwards. Separating them and adding a timer or a sensor is often a one-day job with a disproportionate result, and it is the cheapest item on the Michigan bathroom cost list. Related work sits on tile and flooring, vanity and storage and custom mirrors.

Questions we get asked
Can the fan and the light be one unit

They can, and the combination units at the quality level we specify are fine. What matters is that they are on separate switches, so the fan can run after the light goes off. A combo unit wired to a single switch defeats the purpose.

Is a window enough

No, and Michigan is the reason. A window works in July and gets left shut from October to April, which is exactly when the temperature differential is putting condensation on your walls. Code may permit it in some circumstances; the building does not care what code permits.

How much does adding a fan cost in a bathroom that has none

Most of the range depends on the duct route rather than the fan. A first-floor bathroom on an exterior wall can often go through the rim joist inexpensively. A second-floor interior bathroom needs a run to a roof cap, and in a plaster house that means patching. Expect the upper end of the $370 to $1,050 band plus finish repair.

Will better lighting make a small bathroom feel bigger

More than paint will, and by a wide margin. Lighting the walls rather than the floor, and putting light at the mirror instead of above it, changes how a small bathroom reads more than any single finish choice.

Let us put a tissue on your fan

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits, the electrical and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, or view our portfolio. The whole room is on bathroom remodeling, and the stages are on the renovation timeline. Lighting elsewhere is covered on kitchen lighting and basement lighting.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Tell us what your fan sounds like and where the duct goes, and we can usually price the fix on the phone. Request an estimate to start.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s bathroom lighting and ventilation budget includes the fan and its housing, the full duct run in rigid or insulated flex with the correct diameter, the exterior roof or sidewall cap and its flashing, the switching including timers or humidity sensors, all fixtures specified in the drawings, damp or wet rated housings where code requires them, dimmers, circuit work and panel additions the plan needs, permits and electrical inspection, drywall or plaster patching, paint touch-up, and daily photo updates.

It does not include a service upgrade if the utility requires a new drop, knob-and-tube replacement beyond the work area, or roof repairs if a cap installation reveals decking problems. Those come to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect attached. Where a bathroom is being rebuilt entirely, the fan and the lighting plan get folded into the bathroom upgrade scope rather than priced twice, and material choices interact with the countertop and mirror selections rather than being made afterward.

Bathroom addition
Bathroom addition in Southeast Michigan

Growing families throughout Southeast Michigan quickly discover that one or two bathrooms simply don’t meet their needs, particularly during busy morning routines when everyone competes for limited facilities. Wright’s Renovations adds bathrooms to homes throughout Ann Arbor, Birmingham, and surrounding communities, solving this common problem while adding substantial value to properties. Whether you need a convenient powder room on the main floor or a full bathroom for a finished basement, the team delivers complete solutions tailored to your specific needs and Michigan home’s architecture.

Planning bathroom additions strategically

Successful bathroom additions require careful planning around existing plumbing infrastructure. Wright’s Renovations positions new bathrooms thoughtfully, often locating them near existing plumbing to minimize costs while ensuring functionality. The team considers how new bathrooms connect to your home’s existing layout, creating convenient access without compromising other spaces or disrupting natural traffic flow.

Many Northville and Plymouth projects involve adding en-suite bathrooms to bedrooms that currently share hall bathrooms, creating private retreats that improve daily convenience. Other common locations include converting closets or storage areas, building small additions that bump out from existing exterior walls, or incorporating bathrooms into basement finishing projects.

Full bathroom vs. powder room additions

Deciding between full bathrooms with showers or tubs versus simple powder rooms depends on how spaces will be used. Wright’s Renovations helps homeowners make informed decisions based on actual needs rather than assumptions. Main floor powder rooms prove invaluable for entertaining, allowing guests bathroom access without entering private bedroom areas. These compact spaces require minimal square footage while delivering significant convenience.

Full bathrooms with showers become essential when adding in-law suites, finishing basements as living spaces, or creating true guest suites that accommodate overnight visitors comfortably. The team designs these bathrooms with all amenities including vanities, toilets, and shower or tub-shower combinations that make spaces fully functional.

Plumbing and mechanical requirements

Adding bathrooms requires extending plumbing supply lines and drainage that Wright’s Renovations handles expertly. The team works with licensed plumbers ensuring all installations meet Michigan building codes while functioning reliably. Proper venting prevents drainage problems while maintaining air quality that bathroom fixtures require.

Water heater capacity sometimes requires upgrading to support additional bathrooms, particularly when adding multiple fixtures or large soaking tubs that demand substantial hot water. The team assesses your home’s existing systems, recommending upgrades only when genuinely necessary rather than automatically suggesting expensive replacements.

Bathroom addition design and finishes

New bathrooms should match your home’s existing style while incorporating modern conveniences and attractive finishes. Wright’s Renovations designs bathrooms appropriate for their locations and intended users. Guest bathrooms receive attractive but durable finishes that withstand use by visitors who may not treat spaces as carefully as homeowners.

Kids’ bathrooms benefit from practical materials that handle moisture well while resisting damage from active users. Tile selections, countertop materials, and fixture choices balance aesthetics with longevity that Michigan families need. The team incorporates adequate storage through vanities, medicine cabinets, and shelving that keeps bathrooms organized.

Basement bathroom additions

Adding bathrooms to finished basements presents unique challenges that Wright’s Renovations routinely solves. Many Michigan basements have floor drains below main sewer lines, requiring special pumping systems that move waste upward to main drainage. The team installs these systems properly, ensuring reliable operation while minimizing noise that sometimes accompanies inferior installations.

Basement bathrooms require proper ventilation since natural window ventilation often isn’t possible. Wright’s Renovations installs exhaust fans that control moisture effectively, preventing the mold and mildew problems common in Michigan basements. Waterproofing considerations remain critical, with the team addressing potential moisture issues before they damage new bathroom investments.

Permit requirements and code compliance

Bathroom additions require building permits throughout Washtenaw, Wayne, Oakland, and surrounding Michigan counties. Wright’s Renovations handles all permitting processes, ensuring work meets current codes for plumbing, electrical, and ventilation. The team schedules required inspections and addresses any issues that arise, providing homeowners confidence that additions meet all legal requirements.

Proper permits protect homeowners during future property sales when buyers’ inspectors scrutinize work quality. The team maintains detailed records of all permitted work, providing documentation that proves additions were constructed properly by licensed professionals rather than questionable DIY projects that concern buyers.

Contact Wright’s Renovations to discuss adding a bathroom that solves your Southeast Michigan family’s needs while increasing your home’s value and functionality.

What a bathroom addition costs, itemized

Two numbers stack on a bathroom addition, and quotes that give you only one are hiding the other. There is the shell, meaning the floor, walls, roof and envelope you are adding, and there is the bathroom that goes inside it.

The shell runs $200 to $400 per square foot in Southeast Michigan, which on a thirty-five to eighty square foot addition is $7,000 to $32,000 before a single fixture. Bringing plumbing to a location that has none runs $3,000 to $8,000 on its own. Then the bathroom itself, priced by tier: a half bath or powder room at $7,500 to $15,000, a full guest bathroom at $15,000 to $25,000, and a primary bathroom at $25,000 to $45,000 depending on the county and the finish level.

The line items inside that are worth seeing. A stock single-sink vanity runs about $800 and a custom double with a quartz top runs about $6,000. Frameless glass runs $1,800 to $3,500. A basic shower valve runs about $500 and a thermostatic system with a rain head and body sprays runs $2,500 to $5,000 for the package plus installation. Electric radiant floor mats run $1,500 to $3,000. Tile runs $8 to $15 per square foot for simple subway and $40 to $80 for marble or a designer pattern, which is the widest swing on the page.

Moving fixtures is its own cost. Relocating a toilet three feet runs $800 to $1,500. Relocating a shower drain runs $1,000 to $2,000. Those are market figures rather than a quote, and the full breakdown sits in our Southeast Michigan bathroom cost piece.

Where the space actually comes from

The cheapest bathroom addition is the one that does not add square footage to the house. Before we draw an exterior wall we look for space already inside it, and we find it more often than not.

Five places, in rough order of cost. An oversized bedroom that can give up forty square feet at the closet end, which is how most en suites get built. A hall linen closet backing onto a bathroom wall. The space under a staircase, which is the classic home of a powder room and needs only about twenty square feet with a compact fixture set. An oversized primary bedroom paired with a walk-in closet, where the closet becomes the bathroom and the closet moves. And an underused corner of a landing or a wide hallway.

The constraint on all of them is the plumbing wall. A new bathroom that shares a wall with an existing one, or stacks directly above or below one, is dramatically cheaper than one on the opposite side of the house, because the drain, the vent and the supply are all already there. When the room has to go somewhere far from the stack, the drain slope becomes the governing problem, and that is a design decision rather than a preference.

If the answer really is new square footage, the comparison worth running is against a bump-out, which pushes two to ten feet off an existing wall for a fraction of a full addition. For a bathroom, two to four feet is frequently the whole difference between a cramped room and a workable one, which makes a bathroom the single best value in the bump-out category.

What a bathroom addition needs that a remodel does not

A remodel reuses an envelope. An addition creates one, and three things come with that.

Insulation and air sealing, because a bathroom is the wettest room in the house and a new exterior wall around it has to control vapor as well as heat. Michigan sits in climate zone five, and a bathroom on a new exterior wall wants continuous insulation rather than batts alone, or the cold face of that wall condenses in January when the temperature differential exceeds seventy degrees.

Exhaust that terminates outside. A new bathroom gets a fan sized at one cubic foot per minute per square foot of floor, ducted in rigid or insulated flex to a roof or sidewall cap, never into the attic. Full sizing detail is on the lighting and ventilation page, and it is not optional in a room you are building from scratch.

And heat. An addition is outside the existing duct layout, so it needs a supply and a return or its own source. A bathroom that gets no supply register is a bathroom nobody uses in winter, and a toe-kick heater added after the fact is a poor substitute for a run planned during design. Heated flooring is a genuine option here rather than a luxury, because it solves the comfort problem and the drying problem at once.

What to look at before you spend anything

Four checks, and three are free. Stand in the basement and find where the main stack leaves the house, then work out how far the new bathroom would sit from it. Look at every room adjacent to the proposed location and ask honestly whether one of them can give up forty square feet, because that answer changes the budget by tens of thousands. Read the setbacks off your survey if an exterior wall is involved. Count the spare spaces in your electrical panel.

The fourth is ours. We check the joist direction and depth where a shower pan might need recessing, the ceiling height at the proposed location, and the roof geometry where a new structure would tie in. Then selections follow the sequence on the bathroom design page and the stages run as laid out on the renovation timeline. If a half bath solves the actual problem, we will say so before drawing a full one.

Questions we get asked
Will a second bathroom pay for itself

Going from one bathroom to two is one of the few renovations in this region that changes how a house is valued rather than just how it shows. Going from three to four does not. Our bathroom return piece has the local figures, and the common misconceptions piece covers what people get wrong about it.

How long does it take

Design and permitting run three to six weeks. Construction runs six to twelve for an addition with a new shell, and four to seven when the space comes from inside the house. The plumbing rough-in and the tile stage are the two that cannot be compressed.

Can it be done in winter

The interior version, yes, and that is most of what we build between December and March. Anything with new footings needs unfrozen ground, so the shell version gets scheduled April through November and the interior finishing carries on through the cold.

Full bath or three-quarter

A three-quarter bath, meaning a shower with no tub, fits where a full bath will not and suits most households. Keep one tub somewhere in the house if there are young children or if you may sell to a family, and put it in the room that has space rather than forcing it into the new one.

Start at the stack, not the tile

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits, the plumbing and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, view our portfolio, or look at renovation financing if timing rather than plan is the obstacle. Related pages: tile and flooring, vanity and storage, and guest bathrooms.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Twenty minutes in your basement finding the stack will tell us more about the budget than an hour looking at fixtures. Request an estimate to get started.

Bathroom tile and flooring
Bathroom tile is a waterproofing job with a decorative finish

Bathroom tile and flooring is the part of a bathroom people choose from a showroom board and the part that fails from behind. Tile is not waterproof. Grout is not waterproof. What keeps water out of your floor joists is the membrane and the pan underneath, and that layer costs a fraction of the tile while deciding whether the room lasts twenty years or leaks in four.

Installed market ranges in Southeast Michigan. Simple subway tile runs $8 to $15 per square foot. Large-format porcelain runs $12 to $25. Natural marble and designer patterns run $40 to $80. On a fifty-square-foot shower that is $1,600 at the subway end and $4,000 at the marble end, and the labor difference between them is most of the gap rather than the material.

Two additions worth budgeting. Electric radiant mats under the floor run $1,500 to $3,000, and in a Michigan bathroom that is the upgrade clients bring up unprompted years later. Luxury vinyl plank, where tile is not required, runs $5 to $10 installed and is a legitimate answer in a guest bath or a powder room. Those are market figures rather than a quote.

What actually keeps the water out

A wet-area assembly has four layers and only one of them is visible. Framing and a flat substrate. Cement backer board or a foam board panel. A waterproofing membrane, either a sheet product or a liquid applied in two coats to a wet-film thickness the manufacturer specifies. Then thinset and tile.

Where installers cut corners is the membrane, because nobody sees it and it adds a day. Green board is not a shower substrate. Drywall behind tile in a shower is a failure with a date on it. A pan that is not pre-sloped or not properly pitched to the drain holds water under the tile and the first sign is grout that stays dark.

The corners and the changes of plane matter more than the field. Inside corners, the curb, the bench top and the pipe penetrations are where leaks start, and they get banded or pre-formed rather than trusted to a bead of sealant. Our guide to porcelain, ceramic and stone covers the material side, and the Michigan tile and flooring piece covers what we specify and why.

The economics are stark. Getting the waterproofing right adds a few hundred dollars to a shower. Getting it wrong costs $2,000 to $6,000 in mold remediation, $3,000 to $8,000 in framing repair, and $500 to $1,500 in ceiling and paint below. Ask any bidder to name the membrane they use. The ones who cannot are telling you something.

Grout, and the one specification that matters

Cement grout is porous. It absorbs water, it absorbs soap, it stains, and it needs sealing every year that nobody actually does. Epoxy grout costs more to buy and more to install, does not absorb anything and needs no sealing. In a shower and on a bathroom floor it is worth the difference every time.

Grout joint width is the aesthetic decision people underestimate. A tight joint on a rectified large-format tile reads as a continuous surface. A wider joint on handmade or uneven tile is not sloppiness, it is what the tile requires, and forcing a narrow joint on an irregular tile guarantees lippage you will see every morning. Color choice does the rest: matching the grout to the tile calms a pattern down, contrasting it turns the layout itself into the feature.

On a floor, one number governs safety. The industry standard for level interior areas expected to be walked on wet is a dynamic coefficient of friction of at least 0.42, and a tile that meets it will say so on the spec sheet. Small format helps too, because more grout lines mean more traction, which is the same logic behind the surfaces on our eco-friendly bathroom page. A polished large-format marble floor is beautiful and is the wrong floor for anyone unsteady, which is the whole argument on the accessibility retrofit page.

Where the floor meets everything else

Tile plus mortar plus backer board sits taller than the hallway floor outside the door, which means the threshold is a design decision rather than an accident. The good version adjusts the subfloor so the finished heights meet flush. The cheap version is a metal reducer strip, and you will catch a toe on it.

Inside the room the transitions matter as much. A curbless shower needs the pan recessed into the floor structure, which means opening the subfloor and working between joists, and whether that is easy or expensive depends on which direction the joists run. A linear drain against the wall gives a single-plane slope that is easier to lay large-format tile into than the four-way pitch of a center drain, and it is easier to roll a wheelchair across.

Under a vanity, run the tile through rather than stopping at the cabinet toe kick. It costs a little more material and it means a vanity can be replaced in ten years without a tile repair. Same logic behind the toilet: a floor that runs continuously under the flange is a floor that survives a fixture change.

Heated floors, and why they belong in this climate

Electric radiant mats run $1,500 to $3,000 in a typical bathroom, installed under the tile and controlled by a programmable thermostat. Two things make them worth it here beyond comfort. A warm floor dries after a shower instead of staying damp, which is half the mold argument in a Michigan bathroom. And a tile floor at fifty-eight degrees in February is a floor people avoid with bare feet, which is how bath mats and slip hazards accumulate.

Compatibility is straightforward on tile and stone, which conduct well and do not care about the temperature. Under luxury vinyl plank it depends entirely on the product and the manufacturer’s written approval, which gets confirmed before the order rather than after. Our heated flooring page covers the systems and the controls.

One sequencing note. The mat goes in during the tile installation and cannot be added later without pulling the floor, so this is a decision made at design, not a change order at the end.

What Michigan does to a bathroom

Two climate facts drive most of what we specify. In January the temperature difference between the inside of your bathroom and the outside face of an exterior wall regularly exceeds seventy degrees, and that gradient puts condensation on cold surfaces whether anyone showered or not. In July the outdoor humidity runs above seventy percent and indoor levels sit at fifty-five to sixty-five even with air conditioning. Mold becomes active above eighty percent relative humidity, which a poorly vented bathroom hits every single day.

Which means tile choices interact with ventilation choices. A beautifully tiled bathroom with a builder-grade fan is a bathroom that will show black grout lines in the corners within two years, and the tile is not the problem. The lighting and ventilation page covers the fan sizing, and it is worth reading before you pick a tile.

In the older housing stock around Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti, add a third factor. Second-floor bathrooms in 1920s houses sit on joists that have settled, and the floor is rarely flat. Large-format tile shows every dip, so those rooms get either self-leveling compound first or a smaller format. We check with a straightedge before quoting rather than after demolition.

What to look at before you spend anything

Five checks tell us most of the budget, and you can do four of them today.

Push a straightedge across the floor and look for daylight underneath. That gap is the leveling line item.
Look at the grout in the shower corners. Dark, soft or missing grout means water has been getting behind it already.
Press the wall inside the shower at the bottom corner. Any give means the substrate is compromised and the wall is coming out.
Check the ceiling in the room below for staining, which tells you the leak is not hypothetical.
Find your joist direction from the basement or the floor below if a curbless shower is on the wish list.

The fifth is ours: we pull a tile and look at what is behind it, because a 1965 mud-set installation and a 2005 backer-board installation lead to different scopes and different money. Selections then follow the sequence on the bathroom design page, and the stages are laid out on the renovation timeline.

Questions we get asked
Can you tile over my existing tile

On a floor, sometimes, if it is well bonded and dead flat and the added height works at every threshold. In a shower, no. Tiling over shower tile buries whatever is failing behind it and adds weight to an assembly you cannot inspect.

Large format or small

Large format on walls looks calm and cuts grout lines to clean. On floors it needs a flat substrate and it gives up traction, so in a family bathroom we usually put large format on the walls and a smaller, rated tile on the floor. A Jack-and-Jill bathroom shared by children is the clearest case for it.

Is marble a mistake in a bathroom

Not a mistake, a commitment. Marble etches from anything acidic, needs sealing, and shows water spots. It looks better than anything else on this page and it wants an owner who accepts maintenance. Porcelain that looks like marble has closed most of the visual gap and none of the maintenance.

How long does the tile take

Four to seven days for a typical bathroom, because thinset and grout each need to cure and neither can be rushed. Add days for waterproofing cure time. That is the stretch where the bathroom is fully out of service, and we tell you which days those are rather than letting you find out.

Bring us a piece of your grout

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, view our portfolio, or check current figures on Michigan bathroom costs. Related surfaces are on countertops and shower doors, and the full room is on bathroom remodeling.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. If the grout in your shower corner crumbles when you scratch it, take a photo and bring it. That tells us more than a tile sample does. Request an estimate to start, and the master bathroom page covers the larger scope.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s bathroom tile budget includes demolition and disposal, substrate repair and any self-leveling the floor needs, cement backer board or foam panel, the waterproofing membrane with banded corners and pre-formed penetrations, a pre-sloped or site-built pan pitched to the drain, thinset, tile, grout, sealant at every change of plane, transitions at the door, and daily photo updates.

It does not include fixtures beyond what the drawings specify, a radiant mat unless contracted, or repair to framing and subfloor found rotted once the old tile is off. That last one is the common surprise in a bathroom over thirty years old, and it comes to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect before anyone continues. Where the damage extends into the joists, structural work is priced separately and honestly rather than buried in a tile allowance.

Bathroom accessibility retrofit
A bathroom accessibility retrofit is about staying home

A bathroom accessibility retrofit rebuilds an existing bathroom so it works for someone whose balance, strength or reach has changed. Most of the calls we get come after something happened. A fall on a wet tub floor. A hip replacement scheduled for six weeks out. A parent moving in and the only full bath is up thirteen steps with a 28-inch door.

Market ranges in Southeast Michigan for a full accessible rebuild of an existing bathroom run $14,000 to $34,000. A standard full bathroom remodel in the region runs $16,000 to $35,000 and up, and accessibility work adds roughly 20 to 30 percent to the shower portion while sometimes saving money elsewhere, because grab bars cost less than a freestanding tub. A targeted safety package, meaning grab bars, a comfort-height toilet and one widened doorway, lands at $2,500 to $6,000.

Those are regional market figures rather than a quote. The difference between the two ends of that range is almost always the shower floor and the doorway, and both answers live under your existing tile.

The line most contractors will not tell you

The Americans with Disabilities Act does not apply to a private house. Neither does Michigan’s barrier-free design requirement, which governs public buildings. Anyone selling you an ADA bathroom for your home is using a word that has no legal force on your property.

What matters instead is universal design, which borrows the useful dimensions from those standards and drops the ones that were written for hotel lobbies. That is a better deal for you, because it means the bathroom gets built around the person using it rather than around a code table. A woman who transfers from a wheelchair needs different clearances than a man who walks with a cane and gets dizzy standing up. Our writeup on universal design and aging in place in Michigan covers the difference at length.

The numbers worth holding onto are these. A doorway wants 32 inches of clear opening, which takes a 36-inch door once you account for the stop and the hinge side. A wheelchair wants a 60-inch turning circle, or a 48-inch clear approach at minimum. A shower seat sits 17 to 19 inches off the floor, the same height as a comfort-height toilet, because a consistent transfer height is easier on the body than a good height in one spot.

The curbless shower is the whole project

Almost every accessibility retrofit turns on one decision, which is whether the shower floor sits flush with the bathroom floor. A curb is a trip hazard, and a wheelchair or a walker cannot cross it at all. Getting rid of it means recessing the shower pan into the floor structure, which means opening the subfloor and working between the joists.

Whether that is straightforward or expensive depends on which way your joists run and how deep they are. A pan set parallel to the joists usually drops in. A pan that needs to cross them means sistering, blocking or a structural detail, and on the second floor of a 1920s Ann Arbor bungalow it can mean opening the ceiling below. A linear drain against the wall gives you a single-plane slope, which is easier to roll across than the four-way pitch of a center drain.

Curbless conversions run $6,000 to $10,000 for a standard build, and $3,500 to $15,000 for a custom tiled one depending on size and pattern. If you are choosing between keeping the tub and losing it, our comparison of a walk-in shower against a bathtub puts the resale question in plain numbers, and the bathtub to shower conversion page covers the mechanics. A walk-in shower with a low threshold is the middle option when the floor cannot be recessed.

What else changes, and what it costs

The rest of the scope is smaller money and larger daily difference. Blocking behind the tile matters more than the bars themselves, because a grab bar has to hold a 250-pound static load and drywall anchors do not. Blocking goes in during framing, and it costs almost nothing then and a wall demolition later.

Grab bars, $100 to $350 each installed, with a three-bar bathroom running $400 to $900. Placement gets decided with the person who will use them, standing in the room.
Comfort-height toilet, $400 to $1,000 installed, and worth pairing with a wall-mounted plumbing fixture layout that leaves a clear approach.
Doorway widening, $700 to $2,500 per opening and about $1,200 typical, more if the wall is load bearing or the electrical panel feeds through it.
Roll-under vanity, $200 to $1,000 and up for a countertop swap with knee clearance, or more with a full vanity and storage rebuild.
Slip resistance and light, which means small-format floor tile with a wet rating and roughly twice the lighting and ventilation most older bathrooms carry.

An anti-scald thermostatic valve belongs in every one of these, because reaction time to hot water is exactly what changes with age and with some medications. Heated flooring is not a luxury item in this scope either. A warm floor is a floor people are willing to stand on with bare feet instead of rushing.

Three ways people actually use the room

A bathroom built for the wrong pattern of use is an expensive bathroom that still does not work. Before anything gets drawn we sort out which of three situations we are designing for, because they want different rooms.

Someone who walks but is unsteady needs traction, light and something to hold at every point between the door and the toilet. Clear floor space matters less than the continuity of the handholds, and the most common mistake is a beautiful open room with nothing to grab in the middle of it.

Someone who uses a wheelchair or a rollator needs the turning circle, the roll-under sink and the curbless entry, and they need the door to stop stealing floor area. That is where an out-swing door or a barn-style slider earns its cost, and where a wall-hung toilet buys back nine inches of approach.

Someone who needs a caregiver in the room needs space for two people plus equipment, which is the scope people undersize most often. Two adults at a transfer want five feet of clear floor on the open side, plus somewhere to set towels and supplies within reach. A linen closet inside the room rather than down the hall stops being a nice touch and becomes the difference between one trip and three.

If the need extends past this room, accessibility work elsewhere in the house is worth scoping at the same time, and a consultation is the place to sort it out.

Which bathroom in your house is the right one

The bathroom you should retrofit is often not the one you were thinking of. In the 1950s ranches across Plymouth, Canton and Livonia, the main-floor hall bath is usually a five-by-eight with a 30-inch door, and it is the best candidate on the property because it is on the same level as the bedroom and the kitchen.

In the 1920s and 1930s bungalows around Ann Arbor, the only full bath is upstairs and the stair is the real problem. Sometimes the honest recommendation is a half bath addition on the main floor expanded into a full one, or a bathroom addition off a first-floor bedroom, rather than a beautiful accessible bathroom nobody can reach. A powder room with a stacked plumbing wall is the cheapest place to start that conversation.

If the room measures under 45 square feet, the small bathroom remodel page covers what fits in 40 square feet. If the space is generous, the master bathroom remodel path lets accessibility and a good-looking room share the same budget. Broader work outside the bathroom routes through accessibility modifications, which covers entries, ramps and door hardware.

Timeline and living through it

Design and selections run two to three weeks. Permitting is quick for a bathroom in most of our jurisdictions. Construction runs three to five weeks for a full accessible rebuild, and two to four days for a targeted safety package. The bathroom renovation timeline page breaks the stages out day by day.

If it is your only full bathroom, say so at the first visit. We sequence around it, keep the toilet in service as long as the rough plumbing allows, and tell you the exact days you will need somewhere else to shower rather than discovering it together on a Tuesday. When the retrofit follows a surgery date, the date drives the schedule and we work backward from it. That is a real constraint and it belongs in the contract, not in a hopeful conversation.

What to look at before you spend anything

Five things determine the budget, and you can check four of them yourself in ten minutes. Which way do the floor joists run under the shower, visible from the basement in most houses. Is the bathroom wall an exterior wall, because insulation and grab bar blocking compete for the same cavity. Does the door swing into the room, which blocks a rescue if someone falls against it, and can it become an out-swing or a sliding door. How wide is the clear opening with the door fully open, measured stop to stop rather than by the door slab.

The fifth is ours. We pull a tile and look at the substrate, because a 1965 mud-set floor and a 2004 backer-board floor lead to different shower details and different money. That look also settles whether the plaster is worth saving, which matters in older Washtenaw County housing stock where cutting a chase through lath is slower than framing new. It is also when we confirm the shower door can be dropped entirely in favor of an open entry.

Questions we get asked
Will an accessible bathroom hurt resale

A curbless shower with a linear drain, good light and a wide door reads as current design rather than as medical equipment. What hurts resale is a house with no bathtub at all in a family neighborhood, and that is worth a conversation if you have more than one full bath.

Can you do it without moving the plumbing

Often yes, and it saves real money. Keeping the toilet and the shower drain in place while changing the shower floor and the door is the most cost-effective version of this project. Moving fixtures across the room is what turns a five-week job into an eight-week one.

Does insurance or Medicare pay for any of it

Standard Medicare does not cover home modifications. Some Medicare Advantage plans, VA programs and Michigan waiver programs do cover specific items, and the rules change. Ask your plan before you assume either way, and get the answer in writing.

Should we just add grab bars for now

Sometimes that is the right call, and we will install them and leave. It is the wrong call if the wall has no blocking, because then you have bars that feel secure and are not. We check that before quoting anything.

Start with the person, then the room

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings and the crews are ours and there is one contract for the whole job. See how a project runs, check current Michigan bathroom costs, or view our portfolio. The bathroom design page shows how selections get made, and tile and flooring covers slip ratings in plain language.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Bring the person who will use the bathroom to the first meeting if you can. Their reach and their transfer decide half the drawing. Request an estimate and we will measure the door first.
