Bathroom steam room
A steam room is a sealed box that happens to be beautiful

A steam room is a fully waterproofed, vapor-sealed enclosure with a generator pushing saturated steam into it at around a hundred and fifteen degrees. It is not a shower with a steam head added. Everything about the assembly changes, because steam finds gaps that water never does and it drives moisture into any cavity you leave it.

Market ranges in Southeast Michigan. A steam shower system, meaning the generator, controls and head, runs $3,000 to $6,000. The enclosure around it is a tiled shower build, so large-format porcelain runs $12 to $25 per square foot installed and a frameless glass enclosure runs $1,800 to $3,500. A traditional dry sauna, which is a different appliance and a different room, runs $8,000 to $15,000 installed.

Put together, a steam conversion inside an existing shower footprint generally lands between $9,000 and $18,000. Building the enclosure new as part of a master bathroom project sits higher, because the shower itself is then part of the cost. Those are market figures rather than a quote.

Steam or sauna, because they are not the same thing

Steam runs wet: around a hundred and ten to a hundred and twenty degrees at a hundred percent humidity. Sauna runs dry: a hundred and fifty to a hundred and ninety degrees at very low humidity. They feel completely different, they are built completely differently, and choosing between them is the first conversation rather than a finish detail.

A steam room is tile, glass and a vapor barrier, and it can live inside a bathroom you already have. A sauna is an insulated cedar or hemlock room with a heater, it does not need plumbing, and it more often goes in a basement or a spare room than in a bathroom. Our writeup on home saunas and steam rooms in Michigan walks through the comparison, and if the space is downstairs the basement finishing page is the better starting point.

The practical difference for most households is who will use it. Steam is gentler on the lungs and better for anyone who finds dry heat harsh. Sauna gets hotter, heats faster and does not put moisture into the building. In a Michigan winter both get used considerably more than the owners expected, which is the most consistent feedback we hear.

The details that decide whether it works

Five specifications separate a steam room that performs from an expensive shower that fogs up.

A continuous vapor barrier behind the tile on every surface including the ceiling, lapped and sealed. Any gap becomes a moisture path into the framing.
A sloped ceiling, around two inches of fall per foot, so condensation runs down the walls instead of dripping on your head.
A generator sized to the enclosure volume, not to the floor area. Glass, stone and an unsealed ceiling all raise the requirement.
A full-height glass door with no gaps, including a threshold sweep, because a standard shower door leaks steam at the top and the room never reaches temperature.
A capped ceiling height, ideally no more than about seven feet inside the enclosure, since every extra cubic foot is volume the generator has to fill.

The generator itself needs a home. It is typically a cabinet-sized unit installed within a reasonable pipe run of the enclosure, in a vanity base, a linen closet or an adjacent utility space, with access for service. Most residential units want a dedicated 240-volt circuit, a water supply and a drain line, so the electrical panel gets counted at design rather than at rough-in. The plumbing and fixture page covers the rough-in side.

Ventilation is the part that protects the rest of the house

A steam room deliberately fills a space with saturated air, and that air has to leave afterward. Where it goes is the difference between a spa and a mold problem in the joist bay above.

The sizing rule is different from a normal bathroom. A standard bathroom wants about one cubic foot per minute of exhaust per square foot of floor, with fifty as the code minimum under a hundred square feet. A room with a steam shower or a large soaking tub wants one and a half CFM per square foot, then another ten to twenty percent on top to cover duct losses. The fan runs after the session, not during it, on a timer or a humidity sensor.

Duct details matter as much as the fan. The duct diameter matches the fan outlet, it is rigid metal or insulated flex rated for the purpose rather than dryer hose, and every ninety-degree elbow costs roughly fifteen feet of equivalent length in airflow. Where it crosses an unconditioned attic it gets R-6 or R-8 insulation, because an uninsulated duct in a near-zero attic condenses inside itself and rains back into the fan housing. And it terminates at a roof or sidewall cap, never into the attic, which is a code violation in Michigan and a very expensive one. Full detail is on the lighting and ventilation page.

Where it goes, and what it takes over

The cheapest steam room is the shower you already have, if it is at least about three feet by four and has a solid enclosure that can be rebuilt. The conversion is real work rather than an add-on, since the tile comes off, the vapor barrier goes in and the ceiling gets sloped, but you are not moving plumbing or taking floor from another room.

The next option is expanding into adjacent space. A linen closet backing onto a bathroom, an oversized hall, or the corner of a bedroom are all places we find the extra foot that turns a cramped shower into a room you can sit down in. A bench is what makes a steam room worth having, and a bench needs depth.

Below grade is the third option and it is often the best one. A lower level has the ceiling height question and the drain elevation question, but it also has space, and a steam room next to a basement bathroom or a wet bar turns a finished basement into something people actually go downstairs for. If the sanitary line leaves above the slab, the drain needs an ejector pit, and that is a line item worth knowing on day one.

Timeline and living through it

Design and selections run two to three weeks, with generator sizing and the electrical check happening in that window. Construction runs three to five weeks for a conversion inside an existing footprint, and longer if the enclosure is being built new or the space is being expanded. The tile stage is the long pole, because waterproofing, thinset and grout each need cure time and none of them can be rushed.

You lose that shower entirely for the duration. If it is the only shower in the house, say so at the first meeting and we sequence around it, tell you the exact days you will need somewhere else, and keep the toilet in service as long as the rough plumbing allows. Interior work runs through a Michigan winter without a weather delay, which is why steam and sauna projects fill our January and February calendar. A guest bathroom elsewhere in the house is what makes that stretch comfortable.

One realistic note about after. A steam room wants the door left open to dry between uses and the fan run on its timer every time. Households that treat it as a set-and-forget luxury get grout problems. It is a five-second habit and it is the whole maintenance story.

What to look at before you spend anything

Measure the inside of your current shower. Under about nine square feet there is no room for a bench and a steam room without a bench is a standing sauna nobody uses twice. Then look up: is the ceiling flat, and is there space above it to build a slope, or is the joist bay right there. Then open the electrical panel and count spare spaces, because a 240-volt circuit needs two of them.

Then find the fan. If your existing bathroom fan is loud, undersized or vents into the attic, that gets fixed as part of this project rather than after it. And check the ceiling in the room below the bathroom for any staining, because a steam room built above an existing slow leak is money spent on top of a problem. Our tile and flooring page covers the assembly that goes in once those answers are known.

Questions we get asked
Will it damage my house

Built correctly, no. Built without a continuous vapor barrier or without adequate exhaust, yes, and the damage lands in the framing and the ceiling below rather than in the room you can see. This is the wrong project to buy on price.

Can I add steam to my existing shower without retiling

Almost never. The vapor barrier and the sloped ceiling are behind the tile, so getting to them means removing it. Anyone offering to add a steam head to a standard shower and call it a steam room is selling you a fogged-up shower and a future repair.

Does it add value at resale

In this market a steam shower reads as a premium feature in a primary bathroom and tends to help. A sauna is more polarizing, and it helps most in a house where the rest of the finish level supports it. The bathroom remodel return piece has the local numbers.

What does it cost to run

Less than people expect. A generator draws heavily but only for the twenty to forty minutes it runs, so the operating cost is closer to running a clothes dryer than to heating a room. The bigger ongoing cost is the habit of leaving the door open and running the fan.

Come sit in your shower with us

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits, the electrical and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, view our portfolio, or read up on Michigan bathroom costs. Related work is on walk-in showers, freestanding tubs and bathroom upgrades.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Ten minutes with a tape inside your existing shower tells us whether this is a conversion or a rebuild. Request an estimate to get started, or see the bathroom design page for how selections work.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s steam room budget includes design and permit drawings, permits and inspections, demolition of the existing enclosure, framing including the sloped ceiling, a continuous vapor barrier lapped and sealed on every surface, backer board, waterproofing membrane, tile and epoxy grout, the bench, the drain and its slope, the generator with controls and steam head, the electrical circuit, the sealed glass door and enclosure, exhaust sized for the space, and daily photo updates.

It does not include a service upgrade if the panel cannot take a dedicated circuit, an ejector pit if the space is below grade and the drain has nowhere to fall, or remediation of framing found damaged once the old tile is off. Each comes to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect before work continues. Aromatherapy, chromotherapy lighting and audio are available and priced as options rather than assumed, since plenty of households never use them.

Basement wet bar and kitchenette
The question is whether it needs a drain

Everything about a basement wet bar or kitchenette comes down to one decision, and it is not the countertop. A dry bar has cabinets, a counter, shelving and power. A wet bar adds a sink, which means a supply line, a drain and a vent, and below grade that drain is where the money goes.

This is one part of our basement remodeling services across Southeast Michigan. See the full range of below-grade work on the basement hub.

Market ranges in Southeast Michigan. A dry bar runs $5,000 to $12,000 for six to ten linear feet of base cabinets, a countertop, a backsplash, shelving and lighting. A wet bar runs $10,000 to $25,000, with plumbing rough-in accounting for $1,500 to $4,000 of that, the sink itself $200 to $600, and a dishwasher drawer $500 to $1,200 for the unit plus $300 to $500 to install.

Add a sink, a dishwasher drawer, an ice maker, a beverage refrigerator and a wine cooler and you are no longer building a bar. You are building a small kitchen, and the cost and the permit path follow. Our Michigan basement bar guide works through the tiers, and kitchenette against wet bar settles the terminology. Those are market figures rather than a quote.

The drain elevation problem

Above grade, a sink drain runs downhill to the stack and nobody thinks about it. In a basement, the sanitary line often leaves the house above the slab, which means a bar sink has nowhere to drain by gravity.

The fix is an ejector pit: a sealed basin cut into the concrete with a pump and a vent, which collects the waste and lifts it to the main line. That is concrete cutting, a pump, a vent through the framing and an inspection, and it is the single largest fork between a $9,000 bar and a $20,000 one. If a basement bathroom is in the plan too, the pit serves both and the cost gets shared, which is why the two projects belong in the same conversation.

So the first thing we do on a basement bar visit is find where the sanitary line exits and how high it sits above the floor. If it leaves below the slab, a bar sink is straightforward. If it leaves above, we tell you the number before you pick a faucet. The basement permits guide covers what gets inspected either way.

The dimensions that decide whether people use it

A bar that is too short becomes a counter with a sink. A bar with the wrong clearances becomes a place people stand awkwardly and then drift back upstairs.

Six linear feet minimum for two or three people, and eight to ten feet for four or five stools. Below six there is nowhere to work and nowhere to sit.
Twenty-four inches of counter depth on the working side plus a twelve to fifteen inch overhang for knees, so thirty-six to thirty-nine inches overall.
Thirty-six inch standard height with twenty-four to twenty-six inch stools, or a raised forty-two inch bar with twenty-eight to thirty inch stools.
Three feet of clearance behind the stools so people can pass without anyone standing up.
Eight by six feet plus that clearance if the layout is a U-shape, which is the most social configuration and the most space-hungry.

The mistake we correct most often is a bar pushed against a wall in the middle of a room that had space for a peninsula. A bar people can stand on both sides of changes how a basement gets used far more than a wine cooler does.

Surfaces, appliances and what each one costs

Countertops price out the same way they do upstairs. Quartz runs $60 to $120 per square foot installed, which on a typical eight-foot bar is $900 to $1,800. Butcher block runs $40 to $80 and is a legitimate choice down here, since a bar is not a working kitchen and the warmth reads well against a finished basement.

Appliances are where budgets quietly double, so it is worth naming them. A beverage refrigerator runs $300 to $1,200. A wine cooler runs $400 to $1,500. An ice maker runs $500 to $2,000, and it needs a water line and a drain, so it is a plumbing decision as much as an appliance one. A dishwasher drawer runs $600 to $1,200. A kegerator runs $500 to $3,000 and is the one item people either love or never plug in.

Cabinetry follows the same tiers as a kitchen, and the honest guidance is that a bar is a good place to spend on visible millwork and a poor place to spend on interior organizers. Open shelving with lit glass above and drawers below reads better than a wall of doors. Custom cabinets and custom millwork cover the options, and a dedicated coffee and beverage station is the upstairs equivalent.

Electrical, and the circuits nobody counts

A bar with refrigeration is not a lighting circuit with an outlet on it. Two to three separate twenty-amp circuits is the working figure: one for refrigeration, one for a dishwasher drawer or ice maker, and one for general outlets and small appliances. GFCI protection is required for any receptacle within six feet of the sink.

Which means the panel gets counted at design. A basement bar in a 1960s house with a full hundred-amp panel turns into a service conversation, and that is worth knowing on the first visit rather than at rough-in. A new circuit is inexpensive; a panel upgrade is not.

Lighting deserves the same attention as it would in a kitchen. Under-cabinet light on the back bar, something dimmable overhead, and light inside any glass cabinetry. A bar lit by a single ceiling can is a bar that photographs badly and feels worse. Our basement lighting page and the Michigan basement lighting guide cover the layers.

The basement conditions that come first

A bar is a finish project sitting on top of whatever the basement already is, and in Southeast Michigan that means three things get settled before cabinetry is ordered.

Water history first. Clay soil holds moisture against the foundation and spring melt plus a heavy rain is when a basement that seemed dry shows itself. A chalky white line on the block, rust at the base of a steel post, a sump that runs in bursts in April: any of those means waterproofing happens before framing, because cabinets against a wet wall are a two-year clock. Our piece on what actually works for waterproofing here is worth reading before a second bid.

Then humidity and temperature, because a basement at seventy percent relative humidity in August will swell a wood countertop and dull everything else. Climate control covers dehumidification and the supply register question. Then the ceiling, because a bar under exposed joists reads differently than one under a finished ceiling, and the choice interacts with where the new plumbing and wiring run. Ceiling options covers the trade.

Timeline and living through it

In a basement that is already finished, construction runs one to two weeks. Cabinet lead time is usually the long pole rather than the labor, and on a millwork package that can be four to eight weeks from order, so the schedule gets set by the order date rather than the crew.

If the basement is unfinished, the bar is the last stage of a larger basement finishing project rather than a standalone job, and the sequence matters: rough plumbing and electrical, inspection, insulation, drywall, then flooring, then cabinets and countertop template. A countertop cannot be templated until the cabinets are set and level, which is why the last two weeks always feel slower than people expect.

Disruption is mild. You keep your kitchen and your bathrooms. What you lose is the basement and, for a day or two, some quiet during concrete cutting if a pit is going in. Interior work runs straight through a Michigan winter, which is why our lower-level calendar fills between November and March.

What to look at before you spend anything

Find where the sanitary line leaves the house and how high it sits. Count the spare breaker spaces in your panel. Measure the wall you are picturing and check it against six, eight and ten linear feet, plus three feet of clearance behind stools. Look at the ceiling height where the bar would go, since a soffit for plumbing eats headroom you may not have to spare.

Then ask the honest question about use. A bar next to a home theater or a game area gets used constantly. A bar in a corner of an otherwise empty basement gets used at parties. Both are fine, and they justify very different budgets. If the space is really a second kitchen for a lower-level unit, that is a rental unit conversation with its own code requirements.

Questions we get asked
Dry bar or wet bar

Dry bar if the drain is expensive and the use is entertaining rather than cooking. A refrigerator, ice and a counter cover most of what a bar actually does, and skipping the sink can halve the budget. Wet bar if you will be washing glasses down there or if a bathroom is going in anyway and the pit gets shared.

Does it add value

A finished basement with a bar shows very well in this market, and buyers read it as a completed space rather than a hobby project. It is not counted as living area in an appraisal the way above-grade space is, so treat the daily use as the return.

Can I add the sink later

Only if the rough-in goes in now. Stubbing the drain, supply and vent during construction costs a fraction of opening a finished wall and cutting concrete later. If a sink is even possible in your future, rough it in.

What about a wine cellar instead

Different project, different mechanical requirements, and often a better use of a small windowless corner. See wine cellars, and if storage is the real need rather than entertaining, storage systems costs far less.

Come find the stack with us

We are a design-build contractor in Ypsilanti, so the drawings, the permits, the plumbing and the crews sit under one contract. See how a project runs, view our portfolio, or run numbers with the basement cost calculator. Adjacent spaces are on basement home office and soundproofing and insulation.

Contact us now for a free quote, or call the shop at (734) 251-4187. Fifteen minutes in your basement with a flashlight settles the drain question, and the drain question settles the budget. Request an estimate to start.

What is in the price and what is not

A Wright’s wet bar budget includes design, permits and inspections where plumbing or new circuits are involved, framing, electrical rough-in and the circuits the appliances require, plumbing rough-in for the sink where a drain is available, cabinetry and countertop, backsplash, shelving, under-cabinet and overhead lighting, trim and paint, appliance installation for units in the drawings, and daily photo updates.

It does not include appliances beyond what is specified, an ejector pit unless contracted, a panel upgrade if the service cannot carry the load, or waterproofing and moisture remediation found necessary once the wall is opened. Each of those comes to you as a written change order with the cost and the schedule effect attached before anyone continues.
